Dairy Products, Whey Protein—Contamination Incident

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I wish to make a ministerial statement
under Standing Order 352 in relation to Fonte rra and the potential contamination issue.
Last Friday the Ministry for Primary Indus tries received notificat ion from Fonterra
about a potential contamination issue re lating to whey protein concentrate,
manufactured at its Hautapu plant, that  had tested positive for the food poisoning
bacteria that could cause botulism. Offici als immediately swung into action and they
have been working around the clock since then  to give us certainty and clarification on
the extent of the potential contamination.
I would like to reassure all New Zealanders, as well as our international trading
partners, that the Government has all possibl e resources focused on this issue. We have
established a ministerial re sponse team, and a number of briefings, meetings, and
teleconferences have been held over the days since the issue first came to the regulator’s
attention. Our main priority at this point is public safety. There are a number of
questions that need to be answ ered by Fonterra, and it is li kely that both Fonterra and
the Ministry for Primary Industries will hold inquiries after this situation has been
resolved, but those questions are for anothe r day. As I said yesterday, now is not the
time for recrimination. Now is the time to ma ke sure that consumers have the best
information.
The Ministry for Primary Industries has had staff in Fonterra’s Hautapu plant, the
site of the contamination, conducting testing, and has also had staff in Nutricia’s offices,
assisting with the tracking of infant formula products that may contain the contaminated
whey protein. It has also put officials into Fonterra’s data centres, with its agreement, to
assist in getting absolute clarity on the situation. However, the situation remains fluid.
The information changed a number of times over the first 72 hours. That is why
officials and the Government have been  taking, and will continue to take, a
conservative, precautionary approach until we get absolute certainty.
This issue will obviously have implications  for our export markets. We are working
closely with our trading partners to keep them informed and to get them the latest
information as soon as it comes to hand. Overall, to date the response from international
markets has, on balance, been measured. We have received mixed messages from
Russia, and we are working with the Russian authorities to clarif y the situation. China
has suspended imports of Fonterra’s pr oduced whey powder and dairy base powder
from New Zealand and Australia, and has in creased inspection and supervision at the
border for New Zealand dairy products. Howe ver, that has not stopped imports of our
two biggest exports, whole-milk powder and sk im-milk powder, at this stage. Together,
these two exports to China were worth around about $2.37 billion over the past year.
Yesterday, after the Ministry for Primary I ndustries had issued earlier precautionary
advice regarding two of Nutricia’s infant fo rmula products, Nutricia decided to issue a
voluntary recall for those two affected product lines: Nutricia Karicare Infant Formula
Stage 1, for babies from birt h, all batches; and Nutricia Karicare Gold Plus Stage 2
Follow-on, for babies from 6 months, all batches.  It is important to note the recall does
not affect any other Nutricia Karicare prod ucts. As I said earlier, the health of
consumers is of the utmost importance, and it is critical that these products are recalled,
12294 Ministerial Statements 6 Aug 2013
until any contamination can be ruled out. Parents and caregivers should move to
alternative brands in the meantime, until we can get absolute clarity on the situation.
The Government and officials are work ing closely with the Food and Grocery
Council and retailers to ensure that the two affected product lines are removed from the
shelves, and to ensure an adequate supply of alternative brands. If any parents or
caregivers have any of the recalled product lin es at home, they should return it to the
shop they bought it from for a refund or dispose of it. Officials and the Government will
be keeping the New Zealand public completely  up to date with all information as it
arrives and further clarification is receive d. In the meantime I urge all parents and
caregivers to refer to the Ministry for Primar y Industries website for the latest and most
up-to-date information on the situation.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Our priority today and over the
next few days is making sure that parents here and abroad have the accurate information
they need to ensure that th eir children are safe. As a parent, I understand how anxious
they might be feeling. They are confused a nd worried about whether there is a risk to
the health of their kids. Their questions mu st be answered in full. They must have
access to accurate and timely advice, and not hing must be held back from them. The
safety of our children and children abroad is paramount.
We are standing alongside the Government as it works with Fonterra to provide
answers for parents. We will also support it s efforts to protect our export markets and
the international reputation that  we have from further damage. When the time is right,
we will also be demanding answers, as many New Zealanders will be. Why did the
potential contamination take so long to detect ? Why did it take so long to tell people
about it? Why has the Ministry of Health not  played a major role in getting information
to parents? What protocols do the Ministry for Primary Industries and Fonterra have for
handling these situations, and have they followed them? And what can we do to prevent
this kind of shambles ever happening again?
Fonterra is New Zealand’s largest company. It came into existence under law under a
previous Labour Government. It was given sp ecial rights to operate largely outside the
Commerce Act to maximise our nation’s wea lth, and we are proud of its achievements.
But with rights comes enormous responsib ility. As our only truly global company,
Fonterra’s responsibility includes protecting our reputation as a source of safe, high-
quality food. This is built as much on trust as it is on technology, but the quality of trust
disappears as transparency fades. Fonterra, in  this case, has let us  down. Its strategic
communications have been hugely lacking. People understand that things can go wrong,
but they expect to be told the truth and given the full facts. That is what this country is
known for around the world—our honesty and our transparency. That must never be put
at risk.
Hard questions must also be asked about th e role of the Government. Have Ministers
done enough? Has the Ministry for Primary Industries been too hands-off? The Ministry
for Primary Industries’ mission statement is to grow and protect New Zealand, but has
the push for growing exports overshadowed the cr itical focus on protection—in this
case, the protection of families and their childre n, of our international standing as a safe
food exporter, and of our nation’s overall reputation?
We must work harder than ever to safe guard our valuable relationship with our
trading partners, including Ch ina. China is right to be asking questions of us given
events such as the di cyandiamide scare and the problems with meat certif ication. It is
devastating today to see the Chinese medi a describing our “100% Pure New Zealand”
campaign as a festering sore, and claiming that our food safety issues are systemic. This
shows that the “she’ll be righ t” attitude simply does not cut it in our global market
place. We must be more vigilant than that . This issue is bigger than politics, but
6 Aug 2013 Ministerial Statements 12295
Fonterra is not bigger than Parl iament. It is up to us in this  House to come together and
make sure that everything that happens from this moment on happens in the best
interests of parents and of our country.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I rise to say just a few words on
behalf of the Green Party. The Greens will be playing our part as a part of this
Parliament to find out what happened. I think that is important because we are doing it
on behalf of New Zealand pare nts, but we are also doing it on behalf of parents all
around the world, and that needs to be our No. 1 priority.
Mums and dads both here in New Zealand but elsewhere as well, in other parts of the
world, need to be sure that th e food they are feeding their kids  is safe. That needs to be
the fundamental starting point for anything that we do and anything that we say as a
Parliament. I believe that around this Chamber today that is a common understanding. I
believe that we will all do everything we can to ensure in the first instance that we
locate all the contaminated ingredients, and that we provide all the information
necessary to the parents so that they can be aware of that.
I would also say that I think there is a much  more important role for the Ministry of
Health. I would like to see th e Ministry of Health steppi ng up and providing advice to
parents. The Ministry for Primar y Industries is fine, but it is the Ministry of Health that
I think should be playing a bi gger role in this. We need more information and a much
larger campaign to get that information out than what we have seen to date.
I would also say that there are a number of critical questions that we are going to
need answers to when we go forward and deal  with this issue. Are our food regulations
adequate? Does the regulator have a suffici ently independent and powerful position in
regard to the industry? It is very important, I believe, that the regul ator, in this case the
Ministry for Primary Industries, is in a posit ion where it can control the industry and, if
necessary, enforce standards and make sure that the industry is operating within the
rules that the regulator sets, rather than the other way round. We need to make sure that
that is exactly what has happened here.
We also have a question about whether th e lessons from the dicyandiamide scare
have been learnt. We know that that was, in some ways, the first concern that came up a
number of months ago, and we want to make  sure that we have learnt the lessons from
the dicyandiamide scare.
This is not just a Fonterra problem, and it is not just a Ministry for Primary Industries
problem; it is a problem for all of us. I think that we as a Parliament need to reinforce
the fundamental values that underpin Parliament. It seems to me that there is a place for
the nanny State, and there is a time for the nanny  State, and if that is not protecting the
safety of food that we feed to our children, then I do not know when else we would have
the nanny State. This is exactly when we n eed that kind of State to protect the well-
being of our children.
We have some fundamental questions to ask about the time lag between the
discovering of the Clostridium and the determination that it was Clostridium botulinum.
The number of months between those tw o points in the time line seems to me
particularly critical. I think I have now got my head around why Clostridium was not
found at the beginning. It was found only when it was tested  later to go into the baby-
formula food stream. That makes sense to me, but why the gap between the
identification that there was Clostridium there and that it was C. botulinum? It seems to
me that those months there need more explaining as to why there was such a big gap
between those two points in the time line. I hope that the Government puts that as a
priority in the inquiries that follow this.
Federated Farmers’ Willy Leferink said in the Dominion Post today: “If there’s any
break in this pasture to plate chain then product does not go, or rather, that is how things
12296 Ministerial Statements 6 Aug 2013
are meant to work,”. That chain of custody se ems to me critical to the food security
issues that we need to get right. I look fo rward to the Government inquiry that comes
once we have got through this initial period of making sure that people and children are
safe.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: We thank the Prime Minister
for his statement on the Fonterra contaminatio n scare. This is surely not a time for
political point-scoring, and no one in New Z ealand First misunderstands the gravity of
this issue. This country has always had a reputation for the purity of its food, and
nothing must be allowed to compromise that  reputation, not even statements of human
error. Systems are put in place to eliminate human error when the consequences of such
mistakes can be so dramatic. Our prosperity as a nation depends on it. This food
contamination scare reminds us of how vul nerable our economy is and how vulnerable
the consumers of our products may have been.
Over the coming weeks and months much investigation will go into the how and
why of this contamination scare—how  it happened and why it happened. That
investigation must be comprehensive and th orough. But what we know  already is that a
critical market has been hurt, as have othe rs, and, second, that th e restoration of our
product reputation will neverthe less probably result—almos t inevitably result—in a
price reduction for this product. We also n eed to do some serious thinking on the wider
implications of putting excessive reliance on a handful of economic sectors, and ways to
reduce exposure to risk.
We are also reminded in this crisis that  for our society and economy to succeed, the
private and public sectors must work together, and not just in a time of crisis.
Ultimately, we are, after all, in the same boat.  No one wanted the crisis. It has had great
potential to damage New Zealand’s credibility as a food source, but as a nation we must
use this crisis to learn and build better and safer systems to ensure it does not happen
again.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I thank the other political leaders for joining
with the Government in having as the No. 1 priority that the security and safety of
consumers and, particularly, th eir babies, is paramount. I happen to agree with other
political leaders, there are plenty of questions  that will need to be answered, and in the
fullness of time we will get those answers. I am confident that the Government is
putting all the resources necessary into this  issue, and over the next few weeks and
months we will be doing everything we can to restore New Zealand’s reputation in the
international market place.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. In fact, I have two points of order. The first is a question as to whether this is a
debatable motion.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: This is a non-debatable motion.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My second point
of order goes to the order of dealing with matters in the H ouse. It is my understanding
that under Speaker’s ruling 179/3, the Prime Minister’s correction to statements he
made in relation to a Fairfax journalis t and communications should have occurred
before this motion. It is to be done at the first opportunity. I can understand it going
after the Fonterra matter, because that can ta ke even further priority, but my question is
why that has not been dealt with before this motion.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I now want to refer you again to Speaker’s ruling 179/3. I want to make it
absolutely clear that I am not making any al legation of breach of privilege here. I am
going to take the Prime Minist er at his public word last  week that he was wrongly
advised, and that the errors he made in answering questions in the House were accidents
rather than anything that wa s deliberate. Notwithstanding that, the Standing Orders and
Speakers’ rulings make it abso lutely clear that when an e rror has been made in answer
to an oral question, there is an obligation on the Minister to correct  his answer to the
House. I know that you are in a somewhat uncomfortable position yourself because you
are not subject to oral questions, and assurances that you gave in the Committee stage
are somewhat of a problem to be sorted. Bu t the obligation of the Prime Minister is
absolutely clear. He must come to the House and he must correct his answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! In effect, the member is now re-raising the same point of
order a second time but reinforced with a Spea ker’s ruling. My ruling still stands. It is a
matter now for any Minister—or, in this  case, the Prime Minister—to determine
whether there is an answer to be corrected. If the member thinks the course of action
charted by the Prime Minister or any Mini ster is unsatisfactory, the member has
alternative means to raise the matter.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a further point of order?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Yes, and it goes to what th e alternative methods are. I
understand—again, taking the Prime Minister at  his word that he was in error in the
12298 Points of Order 6 Aug 2013
statements he made last week—that that is not a breach of privilege. Can you inform the
House whether in fact it is a matter of privilege not to do a correction in these
circumstances? Is that the method you are recommending that I take up?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the member can decide what action he wishes to take. If he
wishes to write to me to allege a breach of  privilege, then I would certainly have a look
at that and consider it, as  I do any application for a br each of privilege. But I am
certainly not going to rule on that matter at this time in front of the House without a
formal application from the member.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: This question is to the Prime

items.speaker: Minister and asks
items.text: does he stand by all of the answers given on his behalf to Oral
Question No. 5 on 29 May 2013?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member has got the question
wrong.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! On this occasion, could the member please repeat the
question as worded on the Order Paper.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I made the mistake of using the draft.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We all, on occasion, make mistakes. We do not often expect
many from the right honourable member.
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by all of the answers given on his behalf to Oral Question No. 5 on 30 May

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Now that the member asks, yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Given that his chief of sta ff, Mr Eagleson, told him as
Prime Minister on 29 May of email corre spondence between Peter Dunne and Andrea
Vance, and that Mr Dunne was not comply ing with the inquiry, why did the Prime
Minister state on 30 May that “I do not how Mr Henry is conducting his inquiry.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because that was correct.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Was his chief of staff, Mr Eagleson, telling the truth last
Friday when Mr Eagleson said that he had, subsequent to 23 May, “no further role in
authorising or influencing the release of any further information”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can that answer possibly be correct when it is a
matter of public record that Mr Eagleson was in frequent cont act with Mr Dunne’s
office in the period 27 May to 4 June rega rding the release of email correspondence—a
fact that the Prime Minister has confirmed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What is clear is that whether the emails were released by Mr
Dunne’s office was a matter for Mr Dunne and a matter for his chief of staff. What my
chief of staff made clear was that my expectations were that all Ministers would comply
with the inquiry.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. That last question
challenged the answer to the previous quest ion as to its correctness. The previous
question was related to Mr Eagleson’s claim of having no further role in authorising or
influencing the release of any further information. That is the gist of it and that is what I
am asking. How can you reconcile what he said  with the prime ministerial information
released to the public of the 27 May to 4 Ju ne contact and role and involvement? His
6 Aug 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 12299
answer has no connection to that, though it woul d superficially seem like he had given
some answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The essence of the question is how that answer can be correct, given
some further information the member aske d. Does the Prime Minister have anything
further to add to the answer?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: At the start of the inquiry Mr Eagleson wrote on my behalf to
all Ministers and staff, advisi ng that the expectation was th at they would comply. That
position never changed. If Mr Ea gleson did that, he did that some time before when the
member is asking about.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We are allowed in our
system of government and constitution to ask questions to seek to get at the truth. You
have the chief of staff saying he had no role  at all after 23 May, and the Prime Minister
on record saying that between 27 May to 4 June  all this involvement was participated in
by his chief of staff. One of those statements  cannot be true, and the Prime Minister is
making no attempt to tell us which one is true.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion I do not agree with the final point that the member
is raising. The member’s question asked how  that answer could be true. On two
occasions now the Prime Minister has attempted to justify how he thinks that answer
can be correct, and that is for the Prime Mi nister’s responsibilit y, not mine. On this
occasion the member, I understand, has one fu rther supplementary question left. I will
give him an additional supplementary ques tion to see whether he can tease out the
answer he may require.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I do appreciate that. Does he truly
expect the public to believe that the Chief Executive of the Department of the Prime
Minister and Cabinet, Andrew Kibblewhite , was involved in Henr y inquiry - related
discussions to facilitate the release of phone records and em ail correspondence, but did
not tell him as Prime Minister about this for a whole month?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: When Mr Eagleson said that he had no further role in
authorising or influencing the release of any further info rmation after 23 May, how was
it that he got involved in the frequent cont act with Mr Dunne’s office in the period 27
May to 4 June?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is quite clear. The statem ent made by Mr Eagleson was in
relation to asking Parliamentary Service to authorise the data, not correspondence or the
discussion between Mr Eagleson and Mr Eaddy.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. You will recall that I
used the phrase “authorising or influenci ng the release”. The Pr ime Minister goes
straight for “authorising”, and we all know it  was about influencing the release that we
are after. [Interruption] Well, OK—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: The reality of it all is that, one, Mr Eagleson is admitting
that he was authorising or influencing at a certain date—23 May—and then he says that
neither authorisation or influence, according to the Prime Minister, affected his 27 May
to 4 June relations with Mr Dunne’s office. That is just beyond credibility.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have given a good amount of time for the member to raise
a point of order, which was, in  effect, a debate on the answer  that has been given. I rule
that the Prime Minister has adequately addressed the question that was raised.
Dairy Products, Whey Protein—Contamination Incident
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that he is “deeply concerned” about the Fonterra whey protein
12300 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Aug 2013
scare and if so, is he satisfied that pa rents in New Zealand and overseas now have
accurate information on this issue?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. I am satisfied that Government
agencies are working hard to provide New Zealand parents and caregivers with the
utmost up-to-date information that they have . Parents should continue to monitor the
Ministry for Primary Industries website a nd call Healthline and Pl unketLine for further
advice. In respect of overseas customers, their respective regulatory agencies are
responsible for providing information to th eir consumers. The Ministry for Primary
Industries and the Ministry of Foreign Affa irs and Trade are giving those regulators the
latest information as they have it.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: What role is the Ministry of Health taking to reassure parents that
the baby formula they are feeding their child is safe?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My understanding is that the Mi nistry of Health has been
involved with the response group that was established by the Government. The Minister
of Health has been involved in every tel econference that I was involved in over the
weekend. I might stand correct ed, but his director-general  was involved right through
the weekend in terms of all of the informati on. The Ministry of Health website has been
updated, and we have been monitoring admi ssions to hospitals around the country for
any signs that might indicate that a baby has consumed infant formula that is tainted.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Were Ministers told of the issue before the Ministry for Primary
Industries; if so, what actions did those Ministers take?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My understanding is that at 12.35 on Friday, Fonterra advised
the Ministry for Primary Industries, and then  from there the other contact flowed with
Ministers.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he satisfied that the protocol s—if those protocols exist—between
the Ministry for Primary Industries and Fonterra resulted in timely disclosure?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think it would be very diffi cult for me to actually give an
answer to that today. I think we do need to  go and have a full inquiry. I mean, we have
made it quite clear—or I think the company has made it quite clear—that it was aware
on the Wednesday, and yet the Ministry fo r Primary Industries was not aware until
Friday lunchtime. I cannot explain that gap in time. I think that is one of the very real
issues that needs to be looked at.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that the Chinese media is calling the “100% Pure New
Zealand” brand “a festering sore”, what ur gent action is he taking today to limit the
fallout for New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I think that in reality the first issue we need to do is
actually identify all of the potentially contam inated product and make sure it is off the
shelves and not accessible to consumers. I thi nk, secondly, from there, we need to be
transparent, actually, with all countries that trade with us that we have actually gone and
looked at what went wrong a nd ensured that it will not happen again, and then,
ultimately, we need to continue to communi cate with our customer markets. But I do
think a bit of perspective needs to be put on this. I am not in any way downplaying the
very seriousness of what has taken place, but I think we can also look back on 100 years
of trading food internationally, and we have , generally speaking, very, very safe and
high-quality standards.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister in a position to tell us whether the tests in March
2013 that found Clostridium in those ingredients—and at that point we did not know
whether it was a toxic form of Clostridium—triggered some kind of notification to the
Ministry for Primary Industries and the Minister for Primary Industries?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Authoritatively I cannot be sure, but I think it is fairly unlikely
that it did trigger a response to the Ministry for Primary Industries. My understanding of
6 Aug 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 12301
the way things went is that when they did th e tests in March, I think it was partly done
in Australia with Nutricia. That showed up, they spoke to the company, and the
company did a series of other tests, but it was only really  on Wednesday of last week
when the company was sure, as a result of all of its testing, that it had a potentially very
serious problem.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister in a position to tell us why there was a 5-month
delay between the identification of some kind of Clostridium and the final identification
that it was actually Clostridium botulinum?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, but I think the member asks  a very good question, and it
will be part of the review that will be undertaken.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does the Minister believe that there should be some kind of
automatic process whereby when a food manu facturer, like Fonterra but any other as
well, finds Clostridium in their product, particularly a pr oduct that is destined for infant
formula, the Ministry for Primary Industries sh ould immediately be told that there is a
potential problem?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That might be something that can form part of the review. I
suspect that Fonterra may argue, or other manufacturers may argue, that that actually
shows up more regularly than we think, but , in fact, it depends on the circumstances.
One can only assume that Fonterra itself cer tainly does not want to do damage to its
markets and its customers, and, therefore, if that had really sent the alarm bells ringing
back in March 2013, one would assume that it would have acted much faster than it did.
So it obviously believed that it was not a serious enough threat to stop the production of
that infant baby formula.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Accepting that answer, does the Minister agree that having
found Clostridium, it should have been an urgent que stion that needed answering very
quickly as to whether that was Clostridium botulinum rather than just a harmless kind of
Clostridium, because the answer to that question was critical to whet her it should have
allowed more of the product to go forward into the food chain?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, again, I think the member makes exactly the right point.
We just cannot answer that question toda y. But it does seem very, very odd that
Fonterra allowed production to carry on and fo r that infant baby formula to go into the
supply chain or into the distribution chain. So one can only assume that it believed right
up until Wednesday of last week that that was not an issue. I ca nnot explain why it did
not think that that was an issue, but their sc ientists in the fullness of time may be able
to.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has the Minister put this ques tion to the Ministry for Primary
Industries, rather than just Fonterra, as to  whether the Ministry for Primary Industries
believes that there should ha ve been much quicker action on having found the generic
kind of Clostridium?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I personally have not, although there was a sort of round-table
discussion yesterday with the acting directo r-general, which sort of broadly traversed
these kinds of topics. I suspect those sorts of questions have been asked, but the acting
director-general has been extremely fo cused on trying to understand and quantify
exactly the issue and where th e product actually is. So, as  I have sort of said on
numerous occasions, there will be plenty of time to look at these questions, but it
probably has not been the top of priority in the last 48-odd hours.
Dairy Products, Whey Protein—Economic Impact of Contamination Incident
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What are the
expected economic consequences of the potential whey protein contamination issue?
12302 Questions for Oral Answer 6 Aug 2013

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government’s immediate
priority is to protect families and consumer s in all markets from the potentially affected
products, to share information, and to work closely with our trading partners. In the year
to June 2013, New Zealand exported $45 billion worth of product. Of this, around a
quarter was dairy, and, of that, around a quarter  was exported to China. In the year to
June 2013, the export value of the two products  potentially affected by contamination,
whey protein concentrate an d dairy-based powder, to ou r largest market in China
totalled $125 million. That is around 1 percent of dairy exports, or 0.25 percent of total
exports. Only a fraction of that $125 million of value is currently subj ect to restrictions
into the Chinese market. Products not aff ected include whole and skim-milk powders,
fresh and UHT milk, butter, cheese and yogh urt. There is some longer-term risk, of
course, of effects to our reputation, bu t, if these circumstances are managed
transparently and effectively, we ought to be  able to reduce thos e risks. The economic
impact of the amount of product currently unde r restrictions is su fficiently small and
would not have a discernable impact on our GDP.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What preliminary assessments has he seen of the possible
economic consequences of the issue?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, there would not be a detailed assessment of economic
consequences until or unless there was a likelihood of a significant impact. At this stage
there is no indication that the issue has escal ated to the point where it could have that
significant impact. Treasury advises that macroeconomic effects will depend largely on
the extent of response from our international trading partners, and, of course, that is why
we need to work so closely and transparently with our trading partners.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What do financial market indica tors suggest about the longer-term
effects on the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the last few days I think we saw initially, and
understandably, some reaction both in the price of Fonterra shares and the New Zealand
dollar, both of which declined. We will learn more tonight at the next global dairy trade
auction. Prices for delivery later this year will provide an early indication of whether the
market expects any longer-term effects. Important to avoiding any wider economic
slow-down is, of course, to live up to our reputation as honest, ope n, transparent, and
trusted operators of food safety.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with the statement made by Steven Joyce that he

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: My question is to the
Minister of Police. Is the Government  taking any action in response to the

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

5. TE URUROA FLAVELL (Co-Leader—M āori Party)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Justice
items.text: Is the Government taking any action in response to the unprecedented
recommendation from the Police Association to  call for an independent inquiry into the
conviction of Teina Pora; and does she ag ree with what President Greg O’Connor
describes as significant disquiet among police who are uncomfortable with the fact that
Teina Pora is in prison for this crime?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: There are two legal avenues for Mr
Pora. In 2011 he lodged an  application with the Gove rnor-General for the royal
prerogative of mercy or a pa rdon. This application has b een on hold as Mr Pora’s
lawyer wished to provide additional evidence to be considered. So that is still open. The
second avenue is for Mr Pora to appeal to the Privy Council. The Privy Council may
either quash Mr Pora’s convictions or orde r a retrial, which could result in Mr Pora
being found not guilty. Mr Pora’s lawyer has advised that he intends to apply to the
Privy Council and he is cu rrently finalising papers for this. It is for the courts to decide
whether a person is guilty of any crime—not the Government. It would not be
constitutionally appropriate for the Govern ment to launch yet another Government
inquiry into the police investigation or any other aspects of Mr Pora’s convictions until
Mr Pora has completed his legal options. If  Mr Pora has new and compelling evidence,
then that needs to be presented by his lawyer in the proper way to the proper
authorities—that is, to the courts or the Governor-Gener al. The third avenue of inquiry
that could be initiated by th e Police Association or any ot her affected person, including
Mr Pora, is to lodge a complaint with th e Independent Police Conduct Authority, which
exists for the purpose of independently in quiring into any allegations of police
misconduct.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I appreciate the explanation
given by the Minister—it was pretty fu ll—but I did ask a question around whose
responsibility this is. She did explain that it fell within the avenues available to Mr Pora
and, of course, to his supporters, but the que stion starts “Is the Government taking any
action …”. I am just seeking clarificati on as to whether the Government under the
Minister’s realm has any plans, has any acti on, can take any action, over this case. I am
just seeking some clarification around that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister might like to elaborate, but it was pretty clear to me in
the answer that the Minister was saying it is not the role of the Government at this stage
because there are two other courses of action available.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I can add, I think. I am happy to add for the member’s
benefit that there already is an inquiry, and that is the inqui ry under the royal
prerogative of mercy, which is for a pardon. That inquiry has not progressed further
since 2011 because Mr Pora’s lawyer has said that he wants to present more evidence to
it. Until he does, then it really cannot progress further. So there already is an inquiry.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Thanks to the Minister. What impact does she think the
accumulated impact of the police conduct, the police investigation, and their very public
call for an inquiry into the conviction of Teina Pora has on the general confidence and
trust of New Zealanders in the justice system?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, I think it is a very good point that the member has
raised. The fact is, though, that at the mo ment the ministry is administering 12
applications for pardons and three applica tions for compensation claims. So at any
time—and this is a pretty normal time in these matters—we have 15 claims either for a
pardon or for compensation. This is quite a pu blicly heard matter, but it is absolutely
right in a democracy that  people should be able to state what they think. If they want to
and if they have concerns about any police conduct in Mr Pora ’s case, then I will repeat
what I have said before today—that they should make a complaint to the Independent
Police Conduct Authority, which is the body th at has statutory authority and power to
investigate. I would suggest that if anyone has any genuine concerns, that is exactly
what they should do.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Given that neither an appeal to the Privy Counc il nor an application
for the royal prerogative of mercy can deal w ith the serious allegations now being made
about the police investigation and the hand ling of the case by the prosecuting counsel
and that the Independent Police Conduct Aut hority cannot deal with  both, does she not
see that an inquiry into this matter is now urgently required?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I believe that the member is  getting ahead of himself.
This matter still has an appeal right to the Privy Council and it  also has an open
application for a pardon. So the normal course of events would be that a complaint is
made to the Independent Police Conduct Au thority, which would normally deal with
these matters post any court proceedings, which I think is the correct order. But also, if
the member has any concerns as to the pr osecution behaviour in terms of Crown Law,
then I would have thought that a letter of  complaint on those lines to the Attorney-
General would be the correct course of action.

Dairy Products, Whey Protein—Contamination Incident and Safety of Infant
Formula
7. KATRINA SHANKS (National)  to the Minister for Food Safety : What
information can she provide to the public regarding the safety of infant formula?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Ministers have been advised that
Nutricia has voluntarily recalle d a number of its products to  ensure that potentially
affected stock is off the shel ves until there can be complete confidence as to whether or
not these products are contaminated. Last nigh t Nutricia initiated a voluntary recall of
Karicare Stage 1 New Baby Infant Formula from birth, and Karicare Gold+ Stage 2
Follow-on Formula from 6 months. The Gove rnment welcomes Nutricia’s decision.
Now that there is a definitive recall across the two product lines, the Ministry for
Primary Industries is assisting Nutricia to  ramp up public information. This includes
national advertising of a statutory recall not ice: radio advertising, social networking
advertising, and online a dvertising. People can get in formation and advice from
Healthline, PlunketLine, and the Ministry for Primary Industries consumer helpline. The
Ministry for Primary Industries is continui ng to work round the clock on this issue.
Parents and caregivers should continue to regularly chec k the Ministry for Primary
Industries website for any updates, and call Healthline and PlunketLine if they have any
health concerns.

items.speaker: Katrina Shanks
items.text: What are the main actions the Government has taken to address the
immediate issues raised with regard to the safety of infant formula?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Some of the actions that we ha ve been taking include placing
officials from the Ministry for Primary I ndustries at Fonterra sites in Auckland,
Hamilton, and Australia to verify informati on and to obtain a complete picture of the
products and locations affected by the contam ination. Ministry officials have conducted
a physical check of the plant in the Waikato to confirm the pipe suspected of causing the
contamination has been changed. A ministerial response team has been established for a
whole-of-Government approach on this issu e, and we have been meeting regularly.
Ministers have spoken with food and grocery industry repr esentative members, and
have been assured that they have no imme diate concerns about the ability to supply
existing alternative infant formula. Ministers have also been advised that the industry is
putting in place arrangements to secure the ongoing supply of alternative infant formula
products. From a public health pe rspective, health officials ha ve been an active part of
the response team. The Director-General of Health has been working closely with the
Director-General of the Ministry for Prim ary Industries. There has been increased
surveillance for any symptoms that could possi bly result from exposure of this bacteria.
The surveillance has been in district hea lth board baby units, pa ediatric wards, and
general practices. I am also advised that the Ministry of Health has utilised its system of
conveying urgent messages to general practi ces. This has been a whole-of-Government
response. Ministers and agenci es are working round the clock to ensure th at the public
are protected.

Housing, Affordable—Investment Properties, First-home Buyers, and Mortgages
8. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : Does he agree
with the Reserve Bank that house price inflati on in our largest city Auckland is “rapid”;
if so, what is the Government doing to deal with the demand and price pressures caused
by speculators?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I do agree with the Reserve
Bank, but I do not agree with the member’s habit of calling everyone who wants to buy
a house a speculator; many buyers, if not most , are not. Of course, speculators who buy
and sell houses with the aim of making a pr ofit are already require d to pay tax on any
capital gains. In addition, th e Government has significan tly tightened tax rules for
property owners and investors, and provided the Inland Revenue Department with extra
resources to enforce those tax rules. Thes e moves are expected to raise $700 million to
$800 million of extra tax on prope rty investment every year, which is far in excess of
any estimates of capital gains tax. The Government is focusing, though, as a top priority
on the supply of houses. As outlined by the Productivity Co mmission, regulatory
restrictions on the supply of new housing and new land in the Christchurch and
Auckland markets is a significant driver of th e increases in prices. The Government is
also focusing on reducing the delays and co sts of Resource Management Act processes,
improving the timely provision of infrastructu re, and working with the construction
sector to lift its low levels of productivity.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Would a capital gains tax excl uding the family home dampen
demand from the owners of multiple numbers of houses—if you do not like the word
“speculators”—given that 40 percent of Auckland homes are no longer owner-
occupied?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The “owners of multiple homes” would refer to a significant
number of New Zealanders, and many of them would not  regard themselves as
speculators.

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: David Shearer?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, David Shearer—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —and maybe others. Australia has that kind of capital gains
tax, and it has made no difference. Australia also has restrictions on foreign buyers, and
it has a less affordable housing market than New Zealand. That is why we are focusing
on mechanisms such as the housing accord  with Auckland Council, targeting the
construction of 39,000 new houses in Auckland over the next 3 years. We are also about
to pass legislation—hopefully, with the s upport of Labour—giving the Government the
capacity to speed up consenting, so that we can get more houses on the ground faster in
Auckland.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Did he make representations to the Reserve Bank to exempt
Kiwi first-home buyers from loan-to-value ratio restrictions; if so, why did he not
include such an exemption as a condition of loan-to-value ratios when he gave the
Reserve Bank the power to use them?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Reserve Bank, in the end, will make the decisions about
loan-to-value ratios. The Government has been  consulted and has put the point of view
that was articulated by the Prime Minister publicly several weeks ago. I would say this:
in the same way that the member speaks of having a capital gains tax that exempts most
houses, the Reserve Bank has raised the issue of  the challenge of having restrictions on
low-deposit loans, which might exclude most people with a low deposit. The question
for the Reserve Bank is how to make that kind of intervention effective.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why does the Government think it is fair to give preference to
overseas house buyers over Kiwi first-home buyers by shutting first-home buyers out
via loan-to-value ratios, while leaving overseas property speculators free rein to buy and
make tax-free capital gains?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I simply do not agree with the member’s premises. In any
case, whatever happens with loan-to-value ra tios, the real driver  of house prices is
restriction of supply of houses. Auckland needs 13,000 houses a year, and it is getting
4,000. It does not really matter whether people are first-home buyers, long-term
investors in housing, or owners  of family homes; all their interests will be served by
more houses on the ground faster, and lower inte rest rates than would otherwise be the
case.
Dairy Products, Whey Protein—International Response to Contamination
Incident
9. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangit īkei) to the Minister of Trade : What
reports has he received of international reactions to the potential contamination of whey
protein concentrate?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: New Zealand posts in affected markets
are continuing to liaise with authorities and to share information with them as the extent
of the contamination comes to hand. Govern ments are reacting in exactly the way we
would expect, and most are taking a very measured approach. We have to recognise that
the situation is fluid and that new import re strictions and new testing requirements may
be introduced at any time. But today, as I am answering this que stion, of the eight
potentially affected markets, only one has applied a suspension of  imports. That is
China, and China has been very measured in that response. It has suspended the
importation of whey protein and dairy- based powder manufactured by Fonterra,
including Australian-produced products us ing Fonterra whey pow der protein as an
ingredient. I would just like to add, for members here, that the phrase “dairy-based
powder” is a little misleading to anyone who is not a technical expert. It does not
include our major powder exports. Clarific ation on this point by the Deputy Prime
Minister earlier has indicated th at it is actually a very small part of our total dairy
exports that has been affected so far by the Chinese authorities’ legitimate decision. But,
of course, because it is a fluid situation and it may well change, we are keeping this
under the closest possible review.
The Governments of Malaysia, Thailand, Vi et Nam, Singapore, Australia, and Saudi
Arabia, and the authorities in the separate  customs territory of  Hong Kong are keeping
the situation under review, as you would exp ect them to. Contrary to some earlier
reports, I am advised today that there is  presently no import ban on New Zealand
products in place in Russia, which is different  advice than we received only yesterday.
Our overseas posts are working very closely with the host Governments and the
authorities and regulators concerned to ensu re that these countries have as full
information as possible to protect the heal th of their childre n. I understand the Viet
Namese, Singaporean, and Russian Govern ments have undertak en precautionary
recalls—not import bans, but recalls—of pot entially affected product. Danone has
undertaken precautionary recalls of potentially affected product in Malaysia.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: What measures will the Government be taking to reassure overseas
markets and consumers?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: All efforts are currently focused on the job at hand, which is
consumer health both at home and overseas, as  the Prime Minister and other Ministers
have previously explained. Once we have wo rked through those issues by locating and
quarantining all potentially affected product, we will then begin the critical task of
restoring the trust and conf idence of our overseas markets in the New Zealand supply
6 Aug 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 12311
chain. I would just like to re iterate the fundamental point that the Prime Minister has
made, which is that we have over 100 year s of experience in delivering high-quality,
safe food to consumers in multiple countries, and that is the base to which we will
return. How we, Fonterra, and the other dair y companies that we are in close contact
with manage this situation in the weeks and months ahead will clearly determine how
well we recover from it. The whole of Government is focused on this issue.

adoption laws in New Zealand and put child ren at the heart of all decision making
around their future guardianship. Given that th is is such an overdue piece of work, I

items.text: Why is it necessary for the Care of Children Law Reform Bill to be
advanced at this time?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Our current law in this area dates back to the early 1950s

Commission put out a report titled Adoption and its Alternatives, a more than 300-page
report of ideas and recommendations to modern ise our law and put children at the heart

things like, for instance, wh āngai adoption, which for too long has not been given legal
weight in this country. My bill will begin that process, and I look forward to the support

Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment
Bill (No 2)—Purpose
14. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill (No
2): What is the intention of the Reserv e Bank of New Zealand (Amending Primary
Function of Bank) Amendment Bill (No 2)?
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Member in ch arge of the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill (No 2)) : The
intention of the Reserve Ba nk of New Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank)
Amendment Bill (No 2) is to amend section 8 of the principal Act to give the Reserve
Bank a broader ambit when implementing mone tary policy. This is an approach that
provincial and export New Zealand has been desperately waiting for, for decades now.
The bill would mean that the Reserve Bank w ould have to consider a much wider range
of counter-inflationary measures, which about 50 other economi es are doing, I might
add, as well as supplementing tools for managing the exchange rate—in short, no longer
following the crude prescription for the right-wing monetarists that have so beset this
economy.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What additional tools could the Reserve Bank use?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: That also is an excellent question. Such tools would
include lightening capital cont rols, which would reduce the inflow of so-called “hot”
money, which so many commentators have talked  about, and lead to a depreciation of
the exchange rate, which all the commentators—including the IMF—say is seriously
overvalued, except they do not want to do anything about it. Another option is the
introduction of a cap on the New Zealand dollar and a floor, above which or below
which it must not rise or fall. This would require the Reserve Bank to sell New Zealand
dollars and purchase foreign assets when the dollar reaches a certain threshold, which is
now well past. The dollar has been damaged in the New Zealand export sector for a
long, long time, hence we are finding so many people in the countryside, despite there
being basic primary products like logs, having no employment at all.

Amendment Bill (No 2) help  the Reserve Bank pursue a balanced macro-economic

Zealand (Amending Primary Function of Bank) Amendment Bill (No 2)) : I have to
commend the questioner on his amazing, insightf ul questions, because they are exactly
what New Zealand needs at this point in  time—another very pe rtinent question. The

(No 2) would, in respect of the rural parts of  this country, be of enormous assistance for

example, Southland—with less than 3 percen t of the population and 18 percent of the
exports—which would for the first time in a long time get a fair go. The bill would
require the Reserve Bank to incorporate in its monetary policy th e goal of achieving a
stable and competitive exchange rate, sympathetic to export growth. The effect of a
stable and competitive exchange rate would be a more productive export sector, which
would increase the national income and he lp us earn our way out of the current
economic malaise that the National Government has sunk us to.

members can do with your guidance.

more of the same. It will be more of th e same, only worse: hundreds of manufacturing
jobs being lost each week; more manufactur ing closures, as we see headlined every

farmers sliding into economic difficulty, despite  being involved in wh at they say is the

manufacturing jobs are being lost each week, and the high dollar is estimated to be
costing exporters well over $2 billion a year. We need to have a serious public debate
about the future of monetary policy—in particular, the historically high dollar—and this
time we hope that the National Party, which has so many provincial seats—

Purpose and Feedback
17. BARBARA STEWART (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the
Sentencing (Protection of Children fr om Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill :
What is the intention of the Sentencing (Protection of Children from Criminal
Offending) Amendment Bill?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYL OR (Member in charge of the
Sentencing (Protection of Children fr om Criminal Offendi ng) Amendment Bill) :
How wonderful it is to hear  the member’s question. I must thank the member for
seeking better understanding of what this bill is all about.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Now would the member just address the question.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : I am pleased to inform the member

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart

orphan, whether placed with fo ster parents or kin carers, and that any State support

community on the Social Security (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported
Children) Amendment Bill?

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora. I have been pleased to receive not only substantial
support from the Grandparents Raising Gr andchildren Trust but also positive
recognition from the New Zealand Family and Foster Care Federation Inc. I have also
had conversations with iwi-based social service providers, who have an intimate

Amendment Bill—Timing and Purpose
20. RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First)  to the Member in charge of the Social

finding themselves in the unenviable positio n of being declared  an orphan or an

Dairy Products, Whey Protein—Response to Contamination Incident

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Acting Director-General of th e Ministry for Primary Industries
has issued a statutory statement regarding potentially contaminated products on the New
Zealand market, and the Mini ster of Trade has formally notified the World Health
Organization and New Zealand’s trading pa rtners. An operational response team has
been set up and is updating relevant Minister s. Clearly, this is a very serious issue.
Confidence in the Government’s response is critical. The public requires protection. I
therefore call on David Shearer to move that the House take note of an urgent matter of
public importance.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of a matter of urgent public importance . We were shocked, as a country, to learn on
Friday, through an email or a press release that was sent  out at about 1 o’clock on
Saturday morning, that there had been a serious problem regarding the contamination of
some of our milk product that has been sent  overseas. This has gr ave consequences for
New Zealand. It has grave consequences fo r both our trading part ners and our export
markets overseas, but more important, more directly, and more immediately it has
obvious consequences on women, fathers, a nd children in terms of the formula that
parents are feeding their ch ildren. Many mothers and fath ers around this country are
worried about the formula they had been feed ing their kids because of the risk that
botulism might have been introduced to them . That same fear was spread around the
rest of the world where New Zealand product had been exported.
The response from the Government and th e way that Fonterra responded was of
critical importance to the way that we coul d at least alleviate the many fears that those
parents had. The Government  was quick off the mark. I commend it for its speed in
being able to do that. I believe that the response the Government has made to the
emergency, up to now, has been a good one. But we are still left in a situation where
there are many, many questions that remain unanswered. From the point of view of
Labour Party members, we want to stand with the Government on this issue. This is an
issue of “New Zealand Inc.” It is about our futures together. It is not about politics as
such. It is about New Zealand, our reputa tion, and the reputation of our products
overseas and offshore. So we will stand with  the Government and we will stand with
Fonterra, and we will assist as much as we  can in providing those answers for parents.
But, as I said, there are questions—there ar e very serious questions—about the way in
which this problem emerged and the way in which the Government’s response has taken
12328 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
place so far. As I said, the Ministers have responded quickly, but the question, really, is
about the wider governmental response.
I guess the first question that needs to be answered is why this potential
contamination took so long to detect. The pr oblem was first alerte d back in March, and
it took until now for us to act ually realise that we have sent offshore milk powder or
milk whey that was contaminated with this bacteria. Why did it ta ke so long to tell
people about it? We would have thought that  given Fonterra’s realisation after the
dicyandiamide scare, it would realise that this sort of problem, should it get out, has
innumerable, vast consequences for our export industries.
Why has the Ministry of Health not played  a major role in getting information to
parents? The Prime Minister mentioned that  the Ministry of Health was involved in
some of the discussions, but it has been notable by the absence of its voice in this
particular case. It has not been heard acro ss New Zealand and it has not been able to
give that reassurance. In fact, many of the mothers who have been ringing in to get
good, accurate information have actually b een ringing Plunket. That emphasises, I
guess—underlines—the value and the reliance that we put on Plunket in New Zealand.
What protocols did the Ministry for Primary Industries and Fonterra have in place for
handling these sorts of situations? Give n the dicyandiamide scare and given the
melamine scare before that, we would have thought that protocols were in place and that
it would simply be a matter of  plucking them off the shelf,  so to speak, and applying
them to this particular context. The fact that the information kept changing, the facts
kept changing, is a real concern. There doe s seem to be an absence of strategic
communications within Fonterra that points to some deeper problems within Fonterra
around food safety and the way that it responds to it.
As I said in my speech earlier on, Fonterra is our largest company. It is a brand that
we feel proud of. It is a company, a cooperative, that is  owned by New Zealanders. It is
owned by farmers. It is unique in that sense. It can never be sold offshore. It is uniquely
and firmly implanted in our country. It came into existence in order to provide that clout
on the world stage. Many people have contrast ed the fortunes of Fonterra with the
fortunes of our meat industry, which is far more fragmented and, as a result, is not doing
anywhere near as well. Fonterra came in to existence under a Labour Government,
which had to overlook and override many of the concerns that the Commerce
Commission brought up in regard to the existence of Fonterra. Yet we are very proud of
this company, as I have said. We are very pr oud of a company that has been able to get
out there and be the ambassa dor, if you like, for New Zeal and, for our “clean, green”
brand, and for our clean, green image.
That brand is, I think, about the 22 nd or 23 rd most recognised brand in the world. I
think New Zealand’s “clean, green”, “100% Pure  New Zealand” brand comes just after,
or just before, Dell comput ers. Fonterra was the ambassa dor of that brand offshore
because its products made up 28 percent of our  export value. So an incident like this
creates real problems not only with our milk  exports—which have been shut out of
Russia, there are concerns in Viet Nam a nd Malaysia, and there is the possibility of
being shut out of Sri Lanka and, obviously, China, where nearly $3 billion of product
goes—but right across the world in term s of the way that we are perceived
internationally.
Fonterra is a global company—a tr uly global company—and it has huge
responsibilities. We have given it the right  to be a monopoly in  our country, and we
believe that that was the right way forw ard, but with that ri ght comes enormous
responsibility. As our only trul y global company, that responsi bility includes protecting
our reputation as a source of  safe, quality food. Our food commands the top price, the
premium price, because we advertise it as clean, green, safe, ethically grown, and
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12329
sustainable. It is not born from  large sheds of cows standing in stalls being fed grain or
whatever supplements and chemicals; it is milk that comes from the grass, from the
fields that we are blessed with in terms of our environment and our climate.
But our reputation is built on trust. It is bu ilt on trust as much as it is built on our
technology. The quality of that trust disappears as transparen cy fades. Transparency is
hugely important for New Zealand and the way that we articulate that around the world.
We have a reputation for bei ng the most honest and the most  transparent country in the
world. Transparency International puts us ther e at No. 1. That is pa rt of our reputation,
along with the reputation for being clean  and green. On this , Fonterra has,
unfortunately, let us down in the last couple of days. As I said before, its strategic
communications have been hugely lacking. For me, seeing the changes in response over
the last few days has been very disappoi nting. The representative who was on John
Campbell’s show last night—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Romano.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: —Gary Romano, could not give us a reassurance about the
milk powder that was actually out there on sale—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Karicare

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: —Karicare, thank you very  much—and whether the batch
numbers were at fault or whether the ac tual product itself was the problem. We
understand that things can  go wrong—of course we unde rstand that—but what we
expect from our largest global company is to be told the truth. People expect to be told
in a fulsome manner the facts of the case. As I said, that is what we are known for, and
that is what the people and the Government in China are expecting from us as well.
John Key was in China in April. We have an ongoing relationship with China that is
hugely important. It became our No. 1 tradin g partner in the world just a few months
ago. It has enormous potential to grow even further than that. Our product is regarded
there as the most trusted and the most safe . So when its news agency calls our brand
into question, it creates enormous concern and enormous worry about the future. We
will need to get this right, as Tim Groser sa id today in the House. Over the next days,
weeks, and months getting this right and re -establishing ourselve s as an exporter of
quality food is going to be huge ly important, and the way that we articulate that in the
coming days is going to be very, very important.
After that time we are going to have to work hard to build up the respect and the
trust that have been lost as a result of this  scandal. We have to ask more questions, of
course. Have the Ministers done enough from th e outset? From what I have seen they
certainly have not slackened in  their task, which is good, bu t we have to ask questions
about the Ministry for Primar y Industries. We have to as k whether that ministry has
been too hands-off or, in fact, whether it has not been brought into the loop as quickly
as possible. I suggest that it does point to an issue within Fonterra—that it keeps the
Ministry for Primary Industries at arm’s le ngth and does not bring it in. As a result,
there is a culture amongst some of the more senior people there of, dare I say it,
arrogance—that they know better than absolutely anybody else. Well, I hope this brings
about some humility from that organisation, because that organisation has put at risk our
exports—that is, the farmers in our country —but also, of course , the whole “clean,
green” brand of New Zealand itself.
The Ministry for Primary Industries has al ways pushed to grow exports, and often, I
believe, that has overshadowed the emphasi s it has put on protection. Our biosecurity
and our food safety are two aspects that used  to be quite separate, and they have been
merged into that one organisation, that one ministry. Those two together, I believe, have
maybe lost their way in the bigg er infrastructure of the minist ry. This is one area that I
12330 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
do believe we need to go back to, to see exactly where they were, how they were
brought into the current problems, and what role they actually play, as well.
But our first priority, once again, is the pr otection of families and their children, the
protection of our internati onal standing as a safe food exporter, and our nation’s
reputation. We need to work much harder and much faster on that because this issue is
bigger than politics. But Fonterra, as I said before, is not bigger than Parliament. It is up
to us in this House to come together and to  make sure that everything that happens from
this moment on happens in the best interests of both parents and of this country. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I welcome the opportunity to
speak in Parliament today. Can I start by saying and acknowledging that there are a
huge number of people across the Government and in the community  working hard to
resolve this issue. For gene rations our country has been providing safe and suitable
food. We have an outstanding record, but wh at I can say—and I think I am expressing
what many New Zealanders are feeling at the moment—is that this incident is
disappointing. I want in my comments now to just work through what we know and
what the Government has done in terms of a response. It has been comprehensive. There
have been officials working round the clock, and there is also a ministerial response
team that has been working and has had a number of meetings.
What we know is that Fonterra notified th e Ministry for Primary Industries that three
batches of whey protein concentrate were potentially contaminated with Clostridium
botulinum. Further notifications have been received by the Ministry for Primary
Industries since. The ministry’s companie s and verifiers have been tracing the
movement of this protein and of the products it has been made into, and any
distributional sales. It is im portant for people to understand at this point that what has
been difficult is that the information has ch anged through this event. But what I can say
is that we have had a response team that has involved the Ministry  of Foreign Affairs
and Trade, the Ministry for Primary Industrie s, the Ministry of Health, and a number of
other agencies to ensure that the public have the best information available from what
we have been given.
It has already been in the public domain, obvi ously, that there were two batches that
were recalled by Karicare. The Acting Direct or-General of Health has taken further
actions. When it became clear that the information was uncertain, he took a
precautionary measure and issued a cautionary statement to protect the public, which is
absolutely the right thing to do.
As I said before, there are a number of ot her actions that the Government has been
taking to ensure a whole-of-Government response. Can I acknowledge the Leader of the
Opposition’s comments that this is  above politics. It is import ant, I think, that we work
together across this House to ensure that the public know that we  are operating in the
best interests of New Zealand.
In terms of other actions that the Governme nt and the ministeria l response team and
agencies have taken, officials from the Mini stry for Primary Industries are at Fonterra
sites in Auckland, Hamilton, and Australia to verify information and to obtain a
complete picture of the products and locatio ns affected by the contaminated powder.
My colleague the Hon Tim Groser will soon have the opportunity to speak, and he will
talk about what he has been doing at an international level, because what we do realise
is that it is important that our agencies work to ensure certai nty around traceability of
that product not only for New Zealanders but also for the many mums and dads and the
Governments across the world that have been affected by this incident. Yes, we have a
strong record as a country in  terms of providing safe a nd suitable food, but we have
high expectations of ourselves, and we are di sappointed by this inci dent. It has resulted
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12331
in Ministers working round the clock—whether it is at an in ternational level, through
my colleague the Hon Tim Groser, or domes tically, through me a nd Ministers like the
Hon Tony Ryall, the Hon Jo Goodhew, a nd the Hon Paula Bennett, who has been
involved as well—to ensure that the public are protected.
I can also confirm that in terms of the pot ential contamination of the pipe, Ministry
for Primary Industries officials have conduc ted a physical check of the plant in the
Waikato to confirm that the pipe suspect ed of causing the contamination has been
changed.
I want to touch on another is sue because, obviously, throughout this issue, given that
there was uncertain information, the minist erial response team, Government agencies,
and the food and grocery sector have been  focused on ensuring that there are no
immediate supply issues in terms of infant formula. We want mums and dads around the
country to know that we are doing everything we  can to ensure that infant formula is on
the shelf and safe. What people can be assu red is that there ha ve been a number of
meetings between Ministers—including the Hon Tony Ryall, the Hon Jo Goodhew, and
me—and the food and grocery sector. I want to thank those representatives for their
confirmation to me that they will do everyt hing they can to ensure that supply is
maintained.
This is obviously an incident  that is disappoin ting. It is having consequences, which
my colleague the Hon Tim Groser will talk about. But what I want to assure the New
Zealand public is that we are operating on a basis that is about protecting them, and that
when information comes to hand, we are doing everything we can to ensure that the
information we have been given is communicated in a responsible way.
I am very proud to be the Minister for Food Safety, and I know the strong record our
country has had, but I also wa nt to express on behalf of , I think, many New Zealanders
that we are disappointed with this incident . My focus right now is on ensuring that the
public are protected and that the agencies th at are involved in the operational response
have every resource they need. I am working with my ministerial colleagues to ensure
that this agile response conti nues to work round the clock so  that we have this issue
resolved. What I want to assure people is  that there will be a time to ask those
appropriate questions, and whether they are asked of the companies involved or in terms
of our food systems, I think th at is important because we n eed to ensure that we do
everything we can to restore confidence in New Zealand’s trusted reputation.
I cannot stay here for the rest of this debate. It is not that I am not absolutely focused
on it or do not want to listen to the rest of th e speakers here; it is just that I am spending
every waking moment ensuring that the G overnment response to this issue is
comprehensive and ensures that the public ge t the best information available when we
have it. I have to leave the Chamber, but I just want to acknowledge the Leader of the
Opposition, who has already spoken, who has said that this is bigger than politics. I look
forward to other members in the House wo rking together to ensure that we do
everything we can to ensure that the public are protected, that they have the best
information, and that our international partners continue to have confidence in our
country in terms of our food systems. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party
in this urgent debate about the contamina tion of whey and its processing into other
products. This has been a very confused few days. I want to start by just running over
the time line of what happened. We have cert ainly been trying to wade our way through
the information, some of which has been  good and some of which has been a bit
confusing.
It looks like what happened  is that in May 2012 some  whey was processed by
Fonterra, and about 20 tonnes were shipped to  six customers. At that stage the whey
12332 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
was not tested for Clostridium. That is because of the use that it was going to be put to,
it was not seen as necessary to test it for Clostridium, but it appears that  at this point it
was contaminated as a result of a contaminated pipe, we are told. That was in May
Nothing happened until March this year. What happened in March 2013 was that the
remaining 18 tonnes of the processed product we re shipped to Darwin to make infant
formula. At that point testing of the product for Clostridium was done. This is the
important point. The reason it  was done was that, obviously, Clostridium, particularly
the harmful forms of Clostridium, is very dangerous to have in infant formula. So it was
tested by Fonterra at that point, and at that  point Fonterra established that there was a
contamination problem in this whey that was to be shipped off to Darwin. That was in
March.
The issue I have is what happened between March and July, because it was only on
31 July that it was finally confirmed that it was Clostridium botulinum , which is the
toxic kind of Clostridium—there are many non-toxic kinds. It was only at that point that
it was confirmed that it was C. botulinum. So there is a gap. I think we really need some
answers as to what happened in that gap and why it was only after 5 months that we
finally found out that it was the toxic kind of Clostridium, C. botulinum. After 31 July,
when it was apparently confirmed that it was the toxic kind of Clostridium, things
