moved reasonably quickly. The Ministry for Pr imary Industries was apparently told on
2 August, and then on 3 August the issue went public.
After that there was also some further conf usion. I think there are some issues here
about supply chain traceability, because it beca me a bit confusing to parents as to what
kinds of infant formula they were meant to  be avoiding. Many pare nts, I suspect, went
out and bought the kinds of infant formula that they thought were safe, and it turned out,
as advice evolved over the next few days, that that was not necessarily so.
The primary responsibility of Parliament, this Government, and Fonterra in this
situation is to protect the health of those who are consuming these food products.
Everything else is secondary to that. That ha s to be the primary purpose of all of the
Government actions and all of the fine words th at get said in Parliament. That has to be
where we start.
Locating the contaminated product is essential to that, and making sure that we have
in place supply chain traceability so that we can track that product down very quickly
seems to me to be absolutely essential. I have been a little bit disturbed that we have had
trouble locating some of that product. It would seem that part of the reason, I am sure, is
the 5-month gap between when this was fi rst identified, and when it was finally
confirmed that it was actually C. botulinum, which has created part of the problem for
tracking the supply chain, as th e product has been distributed . We are still hopeful that
the final, remaining part of the product—we have been told that most of it, 90 percent of
it, has been located—is located very quickly.
The next part of our responsibility is about  informing parents from an authoritative
voice. That is where, I think, it is very important that the Ministry of Health is involved.
Although the Ministry for Primary Industries is, I am sure, a fine department, it
necessarily has a different focus from the Mi nistry of Health, which has a sole focus on
the health of people. The Ministry for Prim ary Industries has a more diverse focus, let
us say. I believe it is  important, in terms of informi ng parents and making sure they
have good information, both that the source  of that advice is one that has no
complicated motives but has a simple, straight forward motive, which is health, that is,
the Ministry of Health, and that we make greater efforts to actually communicate that to
people. Not everybody follows the media very  closely every day and keeps track of
exactly what is going on, so I think it is im portant. That is not just for parents of
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12333
children in New Zealand but, of course, in other countries where the product has been
distributed. I believe that should be one of our key priorities.
In terms of where we go from here, ques tions remain for us about the gap between
the finding of the genus Clostridium, the identification of the species C. botulinum, the
toxic species, in particular, and the questi ons we have about why notification took so
long. Are there in place measures, what we  think would be standard notifications,
whereby if a company like Fonterra, or a ny other company that produces food, finds a
potential contaminant like th is? I would have assumed that there was in place an
automatic process whereby Government agencies are notified, whether it is the Ministry
for Primary Industries or the Ministry of Health or both.
We asked questions in the House today—a nd we will continue to follow that up—
about whether there is in place a mechanism whereby there is some kind of automatic
notification when these kinds of contaminan ts or potential contaminants are found, so
that the Ministry for Primary Industries and the Ministry of Hea lth are involved right
from the beginning. That, to us, seems to be one of the critical issues, because of the
time lag involved between the two periods.
We are also, obviously, very interested in looking at the exact relationship between
the Ministry for Primary Industries and F onterra. If you think of the Ministry for
Primary Industries as the regulator and F onterra and the other companies as the
industry, it is obviously essentia l that the regulator has, if you like, in so me respects an
arm’s length approach from Fonterra. That is, it should be that the mi nistry is able to
take an independent position, and step in on th e industry when it is necessary to act in
the greater good. That is the role of the Gove rnment. The role of the Government is not
just to be captured by busine ss, the role of the Government is not to be an arm of
corporations or industry; the role of the Gove rnment is in this case to act as an arm’s
length independent regulator that has both the ability and the motive to intervene if that
is necessary. That will be, I think, one of the questions that we will be asking going
forward.
This issue and this episode have also  raised broader questions about the
diversification, or lack th ereof, of the New Zealand economy. We have seen over
previous years, and it has been a strategy of this Government, a kind of simplification of
the New Zealand economy. That means that we  have become more and more reliant on
a single, large industry. That is, of course, the dairy sector. It seems to us that relying on
a single, large industry has risks, and I thi nk those risks have been exposed during this
period. It does not result in a highly resilient economy; it results, in some respects, in a
more fragile economy.
We would argue that this case should be a wake-up call for all of us that we need to
diversify not only the New Zealand economy mo re broadly but also the primary sector.
We should not have just a primary sector th at is leaning so h eavily on dairy, and we
should not have an export sector more gene rally and a tradable se ctor more generally
that are leaning so heavily on dairy. We think it is very important that we develop the
manufacturing sector and that we develop the other sectors of the economy, such as the
information and communications technology sect or, so that we do not simply rely on
one large industry, which, if something goes aw ry and that industry gets into trouble,
has significant effects on the New Zealand economy.
We think also that this case does bring home to us the significance and importance of
“clean, green, and safe” as the branding of the New Zealand agrifood industry and, of
course, of New Zealand as a whole. That  branding of “clean, green, and safe” is
incredibly valuable, and if we push toward s more and more quantity or volume through
the sector, and in the process compromise “cle an, green, and safe”, then I think that is a
significant problem for our export sector. Obviously, we do not know the details of how
12334 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
exactly this problem evolved, but it certainly  has brought to the fore how critical those
reputational issues are,  and how it is very important that  we protect them, in order to
protect not just the long-term interests of the dairy sector and the agrifood sector but the
long-term interests of New Zealand more broadly.
At the end of my contribution, I will just return to the importance of staying focused
on the food and those who consume it. That ha s to be our primary concern. That has to
be the concern of the Government. All the other issues around the development of the
dairy sector, in terms of fi nding out what happened, are all very important, but in the
first instance our focus needs to remain on making sure that we track down that food
and that we notify those parents of the issues involved. That needs to be, at this point in
time, our No. 1 focus, and then in time we will be looking at exactly why this happened.
Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise on behalf of Ne w Zealand First to make a
contribution in this very serious urgent debate, which doubtless affects us all. There can
be no dispute that the Fonterra food contamination scare is a very, very serious matter
for New Zealand. As a parent, there is nothing you care more about in the world than
your child’s welfare. Every pa rent in this House would ag ree with me on that, I am
certain. Our immediate concern therefore has to  be with the families and their children
who may have been affected by this issue, and we must act in a cooperative manner as a
Parliament to address that. We stand w ith the Government and with the Opposition—
the Labour Opposition—in this regard. This is a time for questions, certainly, but not
yet a time for recriminations. Questions will follow, and from them we certainly hope
there will be answers so that situations like this are not rep eated. How many children
have been affected? One has to  assume that there is a huge  number potentially affected
here and abroad. The news that Nutricia Karicare Stage 1 New Baby Infant Formula,
which is for babies from birth, and Nutricia Karicare Gold+ Stage 2 Follow-on Formula,
which is for babies from 6 months, have b een affected, or may ha ve potentially been
affected, by this contaminated powder is truly shocking.
It is important to remember that when child ren are involved in an issue such as this,
the world takes notice. This story has been covered in news agencies not just in the
countries affected but further afield, in the United States and in the United Kingdom. It
has been covered across th e Asian continent, from The Times of India  to the Bangkok
Post, the Taipei Times , all the way to Saudi Arabia  and the Middle East. The BBC,
CNN, the  Wall Street Journal , the New York Times , the Financial Times , and
Australia’s the Age and the  Sydney Morning Herald  have all covered the story. All of
these markets and all of these parents are seeing the news that New Zealand products
are potentially dangerous for children.
Our whole economy hinges on our capacity to supply our export markets with pure
food. That has been one of our great compar ative advantages in a world that seeks
healthy food. I can speak from personal expe rience, from 10 years in the wine industry,
of the degree of attention th at has to be paid to cleanlin ess, and the degree to which
people have to be absolutely fastidious at  all stages in the food production chain. As a
winemaker, it was my responsibility to make sure that there was no contamination at all
entering the wine. In fact, cont amination at any stage could have resulted in the product
being destroyed. Even if the product was not destroyed, there were residues. I remember
one occasion particularly where a competitor winery had an instance where they had not
observed a withholding period for an application of fungi cide in a vineyard, and a
residue of a banned fungicide was detected in  a consignment of wine that was exported
to the European Union. The Europeans, of course, have extremely stringent controls and
safety standards for chemicals of that type. The end result was that an entire shipment
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12335
was written off. That resulted in extreme fina ncial hardship for that particular winery,
which resulted in it going broke.
So, in one way, this food contamination s care is a wake-up call for all of us. Any
illusions of complacency that we might have had have been dispelled. It reminds us of
how vulnerable our economy is. So it will be vital to get to the heart of this matter—
when, why, and how it happened. New Zeal and First is of the view that serious
questions will need to be asked of the whol e role that Fonterra plays in our economy.
We do have a lot of eggs in one basket. We place a lot of faith in Fonterra as a large
player on the global scene, but I thi nk we lull ourselves into a sense of
misunderstanding about Fonterra and its size in the world dairy market. In New Zealand
we allow ourselves to believe that we are a major and significant player in dairy in
global terms because of the size of our exports relative to production. We know, for
example, that New Zealand—mostly thr ough Fonterra—supplies something like 35
percent of the world’s cross- border trade in dairy produc ts, and, for that reason, we
believe ourselves to be massively significant.
The reality is, however, that New Zealand produces less than 3 percent of the world’s
milk. Most of the world’s dairy production is  consumed in the country of origin. Where
New Zealand has an advantage is that we have an enormous cap acity for production,
over and above what our own requirements for consumption are. So that puts us in a
position where we are able to export 95 perc ent of what we produce. That is a good
thing because it gives us a strong underpinning to our economy, but it also puts us in a
position where, if a scare like this happens, we are reliant on the preservation of our
brand’s business—of Fonterra’s brand’s busin ess particularly—because there is not the
sheer volume or bulk of other commodities to  back it up. Countries that seek these
products can get them from other places.
So maybe we have too many eggs in the one basket. With size comes economies of
scale, and efficiency is one of those thin gs, but there is a down side, and that is
increased vulnerability. The balance needs to  be the right one. We must rethink our
approach to risk, given the role of the da iry sector. Fonterra is a global company, but
along with the gains that come from globali sation, there is immense responsibility. New
Zealand First will not rush to judgment on th is crisis, but we would ultimately like to
see some good come of it. That means that th e following need to be addressed: firstly,
that this type of situation is not repeated; secondly, that our systems emerge stronger
and more robust; and, thirdly, that New Zeala nd does get credit for dealing directly and
openly with this crisis.
I think it is pertinent to point out at this point that at the moment we have a scare—a
scare relating to a pot ential contamination of a very sm all quantity of one product line
from one company. In the fullness of time it will probably turn out that, in actual fact,
nobody has been hurt by it. But one thing th at has been hurt is New Zealand’s
reputation, and the reputation of  our premium brands has been hurt. We will work hard
and we will get that reputation back, but it is also worthy of note that in some markets
the efforts that we undertake in order to ensu re that we do regain our premium place in
those markets mean that those markets will offer us a correspondingly lower price,
because they realise that there is that element of risk and they realise that there is that
great element of importance to us.
I think it is probably a good time for us to consider that we have this enormous
potential for effect on our entire econo my—on brand New Zealand, on “New Zealand
Inc.”—as a result of one scare from one small potential contamination from one product
from one line. I ask the House whether we ha ve given consideration to what the effects
on our economy would be if a disaster were to  occur on a much greater scale, and if we
were faced with a genuine problem around an issue such as foot-and-mouth disease. I
12336 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
think this scare over possible contamination should serve as a canary in the mine shaft
to New Zealand. It should serve as a warning as to how vulnerable we are, as to how
vulnerable our export-based economy is, and as to how vulnerable all of us are here in
New Zealand if our primary sector is th reatened. I think it is  a good time for New
Zealand to look at our biosecurity systems. This wake-up call of an organism potentially
leaving New Zealand gives us cause to wonder what would happen if an unwanted
organism was to enter New Zealand. New Zeal and First is on record as saying that we
believe that this Government’s  approach to biosecurity means that foot-and-mouth is a
matter of when and not if, and when that day comes, that will be truly disastrous for us
all.
I reiterate that New Zealand First does not rush to judgment on this crisis. We do
stand with the Government and with the Opposition in standing with Fonterra, and
ensuring that we do have a resolution to this issue as soon as possible. But I think that at
the same time it is necessary for us all to give serious consideration to how severe an
outbreak could be. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Like others across the House—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: This is a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Like others across the
House, I say that no one would wish this day to have come. This is about “New Zealand
Inc.” This is about an indus try that is 26 percent of Ne w Zealand’s exports with 35,000
workers plus an estimated 10,000 self-employed, we believe. I thank the Government
for its response, but, like others, I say that it seems to us as observers—and these are
questions for another day—that if it is the case that Minister s were blind-sided, as they
possibly appear to have been, then substantial questions need to be answered in coming
days and weeks, once we are through this crisis, as to where we got to in the last few
days.
This is about, firstly, as others have sa id, the safety of the smallest individuals—
children—both in New Zealand and in other ju risdictions. We have to continue to do
everything that is humanly possible to ensure that that safety continues and that children
do not fall foul, either in our jurisdiction or internationally, of the difficulties that we are
now in with these milk products.
Equally linked to that, of course, is New Zealand’s intern ational reputation. A
reputation can be destroyed in this day and age in a millisecond and can take months, if
not years, of work to restore by both the G overnment and the priv ate sector. The only
way we maintain and enhance that reputa tion is by ensuring that our international
markets and those Governments and regulators in foreign jurisdicti ons have trust and
confidence that we will communicate clearly, that we will communicate consistently,
that we will do all that is within our power—and I include in these comments, of course,
Fonterra—to ensure that these matters are remedied.
I welcome the Government’s response in response to th e Labour Party and
Opposition parties’ comments that this is a bove politics and, of c ourse, it is. There are
times in this Parliament where we need to rise above politics, when the national interest
is at stake, and one could argue in fiscal te rms that the national interest is indeed at
stake. I would say in response to Minister Ka ye and to Minister Groser that it may well
be appropriate, given the non-partisan nature that we have over this issue, that they may
wish to extend to Opposition parties briefings about these particular issues we have in
common. To date that has not occurred. We know that there have been other and greater
priorities, and I acknowledge those, but I say to those Minister s that if we are serious in
joining together to resolve this, then those briefings are important.
Can I make one other comment, and again it is a matter for coming days, but there
needs to be, as others have said, a full, open,  and transparent set of inquiries into these
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12337
matters. I note, I believe from either a Mini ster or the Prime Minister’s response today,
that the feeling is that there should be a Fonterra inquiry and a Ministry for Primary
Industries inquiry. Can I make the suggestion to those Ministers that that is all well and
good, but if we are trying to restore confidence in foreign jurisdictions, I think it will be
necessary for an independent form of inquiry that goes beyond the Government
department and that goes beyond Fonterra. I th ink that, given the publicity that is in the
China Daily Mail and others, it would not be accepta ble for Fonterra to be inquiring
into itself, or for the Government department  to inquire into itsel f. There needs to be
somebody of standing, somebody outside those regimes, who can make a full account of
the facts, put that in a transparent way, and put that account before Parliament and the
people of New Zealand, and enable Minister Groser and others to take that out to
foreign jurisdictions and give assurances th at are independently verified that these
matters will be resolved and will not occur again.
Can I say, finally, to those in Fonterra that they will need to look very, very carefully
at their conduct over this i ssue given melamine, given dicy andiamide, and given this.
They must explain, they must communicate, an d they must be consistent not only to the
parents in New Zealand and foreign jurisdic tions but also to international markets.
Sadly, I think they have been found wanting.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: First of all, I w ould just like to
acknowledge to my colleague Mr Cosgrove th at I have taken very careful note of your
constructive suggestions. You will understand that I cannot go beyond that. I think all of
us understand that there is a very high degr ee of unanimity in this House on this matter,
and I think that it has got certain common elem ents to it. The first and most important
common element coming through clearly from  all of the leader s’ speeches and
subsequent comments that we have just heard in this snap debate is a deep concern for
the very, very young children who could be affected. Thank God we have not heard
reports of that so far. Also, so closely asso ciated with that is deep concern for their
parents, their caregivers, their grandparents , their relatives, and a ll of these people who
worry about these little people, because of  the intense emotional bond that you feel to
one of your own at that age.
Rather than talk about this in generalities, I would like to  talk about it specifically. I
do not know whether members noticed, but half an hour ago I was in the visitors gallery
with two of my own little mokopuna, Lucia a nd Sophia—reflecting the Italian heritage
of part of my wider family. They are visiting me, their grandpa, from Hong Kong. The
elder little girl was about 8 months old wh en the disaster in 2008 occurred over milk
poisoning, and I had just been appointed, informally, Minister  of Trade to replace my
parliamentary colleague Phil Goff, and wa s sent on a plane to the APEC leaders
meeting. At that stage we did not know wh ether it was New Zealand milk. We did not
know what the cause of it was. Just before I got on the plane, my daughter-in-law, who
was also up there half an hour ago, rang me and said: “C ongratulations on becoming a
Minister. Now you are the Minister of Trad e, you’ve got to do something about this,
because I can’t find infant formula fo r your granddaughter.”—who was the child up
there.
So I went to make an appointment with the Chinese Minister of Commerce, Chen
Deming, who would also be very well-known to Mr Goff, and at the end of this
discussion, in which neither of us really knew what was going on, other that dozens of
babies in China were going to hospital with renal failure, for reasons that neither of us
really knew at the time, I told him this story in slightly more diplomatic terms. And he
paused and he said: “This is  extraordinary, because I have just received the same phone
call about one of my granddaughters.” It is  moments like that when you realise how
12338 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
completely trivial positions are and that, at the end of the day, human beings are
speaking to human beings across cultures with exactly the same concerns.
Members will appreciate that I have trie d to do what I can for the parents and
caregivers of children in China today. I have been speaking to China Central Television,
one of the main Chinese television ch annels, trying to c onvey our sympathy and
understanding for the uncertainties of the situ ation they are in. But I do think we should
acknowledge that this is a ve ry testing time for the careg ivers of these children. As I
say, thank God we have not heard of any illness so far, but, for technical reasons that I
do not really have time to go into, you shoul d not read too much optimism into that
statement because of the delays that can occur under certain clinical conditions.
I do appreciate that members outside a small group of Minist ers—well, not that
small; eight Ministers are involved in this—have not been briefed properly by us for the
reasons that Mr Cosgrove was alluding to, fully understanding the need for priorities
here. But one thing that I can put to rest im mediately is that the Director-General of
Health and his senior officials have been in timately involved in this. The front face in
terms of the media has been the Director-G eneral, but I can assure members that the
Ministry of Health is deep ly involved, and I personally he ard the Director-General in
one of our teleconferences at  least once with his technica l advisers talking about the
health aspects of this. This will slowly emerge  as we are able to have more time to brief
people more fully on these issues.
In the very brief time that I have left, just  let me assure members that in terms of my
part in this puzzle, I will l eave no stone unturned to try to both deal with the immediate
human concerns of our customers and then contain the economic damage to our country
for all the reasons that are stunningly obvious. Just to make one final concluding
comment, I am optimistic that with the proud record of this country—we are a small but
sophisticated country—we will find our way through. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Thanks for the
opportunity to make some comments this afte rnoon in what is a very important debate.
It is important because of health and safety and food security. It is also important for our
exports and, overall, our economy.
I think it is important to remind everyone in the House that our primary sector
exports make up about 72 percen t of our total merchandise exports and are, indeed, a
crucial part of the New Zealand econom y. As a small country of around 4.5 million
people, food production is hugely important to  us. We feed about 40 million people and
we export to almost 200 countries around th e world. We have been renowned for our
food production, and, indeed, over about a century we have b een exporting some of the
finest food products to all of these different parts of the planet. Of course, that is
underpinned by our high-quality food safety sy stems, biosecurity, animal welfare, and,
indeed, environmental management. They all form a part of underpinning our exports to
almost 200 countries around the world.
Importantly, when you get out from New Zealand—and I have been lucky enough to
go on a couple of trade missions this year: one to Latin America with the Prime
Minister, and one when I led a delegati on to China recently—when you look back at
New Zealand, and when you are in other countr ies and you hear them  talk about all of
those things that I have just talked about, they are fundamentally important to exporters.
We need to ensure that we do the utmost to hold up our integrity on the world stage as
the producer of some of the best and finest food in the world.
Importantly, this particular incident that we are discussing in the House this
afternoon is disappointing. It is disappoint ing that it has occurred. Consumers are
disappointed, the Government is disappointe d, our trading partne rs are disappointed,
and our hard-working farmers, who get up at  4 a.m. or 5 a.m. every morning and
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12339
produce a high-quality food product, are disappointed as well. We will, however, get
through this. It will knock our reputation around a bit, but we will be stronger. We will
be stronger as a country from this event into the future.
There are a whole lot of questions that we  all want to ask a nd, indeed, we want
answers to, and at the appropriate time we will be able to get the answers to those
questions that we all so desire. Right now, the focus is on the health and well-being of
our children, particularly, and our families,  and I want to acknowledge the work that
Minister Kaye, Minister Rya ll, and Minister Goodhew have done in this space. I also
want to acknowledge the work that Minister Groser has don e on the international stage
in reaching out to our markets.
The response across the Government has,  I believe, shown to the New Zealand
public how importantly we have treated this  issue from when Ministers became aware
of it on Friday afternoon. We set up a mini sterial group. Official s from a number of
agencies have come together and, indeed, have worked all weekend. I have been
impressed by our all-of-Government approach and, indeed, I have been keeping in touch
with the industry, and its response has been consistent. Food safety is the top priority for
New Zealand, and we need to do what we can  to assure New Zealanders and our export
markets that we are taking this very, very seriously.
The industry groups have expressed deep di sappointment that this has happened, but
they are committed to doing what they can to assure New Zealanders and overseas
markets that, as an exporting food nation, we  treat these food safe ty issues extremely
seriously. We will get through this. We will be stronger for it. Thank you for the
opportunity to make a contribution this afternoon on what is a very important issue.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Well, right from the earliest
moments of this incident, our first thoughts were for the safety and security of our food.
In our health portfolio roles, both Minister  Ryall and I were intricately involved right
from the beginning, and it very quickly beca me apparent that our most vulnerable
citizens—our youngest children—woul d be those most at risk if their milk formula
powder should be contaminated with Clostridium botulinum. From the earliest time on
Friday, as other Ministers have expresse d, Ministers from across portfolios joined
together to look from all angles at how we  could work our way through this incident—
the Minister for Food Safety, Nikki Kaye; th e Minister for Primar y Industries, Nathan
Guy; Minister Ryall and me; and the forei gn affairs and trade Ministers McCully and
Groser, along with other senior Ministers.
I want to say right now that I feel for the families who, through this time, have
worried about what information should be in front of them. Those parents are of course
hungry for information, and it would be fair to  say that as information has changed and
as the information put before the Ministry  for Primary Industries has improved in its
quantity and quality, then more information has been able to be conveyed to parents. As
many members here in the House will know, two products have now been recalled. I
want to lay on the record of the House t oday, again, the names of those two products:
Nutricia Karicare Stage 1 New Baby Infant Formula—that is, from birth—all batches,
and Nutricia Karicare Gold+ Stage 2 Follow- on Formula, from 6 months, all batches.
There is a recall currently under way. I urge any families using those products to return
them to the place of purchase.
In terms of the role of the Ministry of Hea lth, its role has been to maintain vigilance
regarding any possible cases of infant botulism, and I want to just remind the House of
the symptoms that people should be looking out  for: poor feeding or a weak suck on the
part of a baby or toddler, lethargy and floppi ness, a weak cry, facial weakness, and an
impaired gag reflex. But, in essence, if th ere are any concerns on the part of a parent,
they should ring PlunketLine or Healthline, or take their child to a doctor. In terms of
12340 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
Healthline and PlunketLine, we ll, their volumes have increa sed significantly. That tells
me that our messages about the phone numbe rs, which are consistently going out via
websites and other media, have been hear d. Yesterday PlunketLine had 1,500 calls. It
has done a wonderful job, as has Healthline, of gearing up the numbers of people who
are taking shifts to respond to the increased numbers of calls coming to it for the advice
that families so eagerly seek. I just want to  actually thank those people who are staffing
those lines for the extra work that I know they have done.
In terms of the other roles the Ministry of Health has,  they are around working to
ensure the adequacy of supply, and that includes the adequacy of supply to our
paediatric units, our baby-care units, and, in addition to that, maintaining the
information that goes out to general practices , so that the doctors whom families go to
for advice are also completely up to date w ith what they need to know. These are the
roles that the Ministry of Health has undert aken. It has sat at th e table, through the
Director-General and his senior deputy dire ctors-general. They are sitting round the
table, keeping Ministers informed, and working with the Ministry for Primary
Industries. This is a concerted, united front, so that we can present the very best of
information to the public of New Zealand,  to reassure those families who will be
concerned with the most up-to-date information that we have before us. So I just want
to finish by thanking all of the people within the health sector who have done their bit to
reassure those families and to say to the H ouse that we are really hoping that soon the
families will be able to look back on this and be sure that their babies are fine.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : Kia ora to the
people in the gallery. Like many people in this House, I am a parent. I am the father of
five beautiful daughters, and although I am a gr eat advocate of “Breast is best”, I, like
most parents, have relied on infant formula to sustain our helpless but beautiful babies.
We have got up in the middle of the night to mix the formula to make the milk. That is
the only thing that our infant babies live on. That is why, around the world, people have
reacted so strongly to this. It is an emotional issue—what we feed our children—and we
should realise that. No parent should make any apology for being concerned.
I have been a dairy farmer. I can appreciate the effort that goes in to providing clean
and pure milk to the company. I was also the chairman of a select committee that set up
Fonterra back in the year 2000. So I understand that companies set up through the
legislation had some advantages, but they  also had with the legislation clear
responsibilities. Fonterra was to be, of course, given its size and importance to our
economy, the guardian of a reputation that ha d been built up by generations of people
that the dairy industry produced the safest and best food in the world. As the primary
industry spokesperson on behalf of the Labour Party, I am  now supporting the
Government and supporting Fonterra to get out around the world a nd reassure all our
customers that the food that we produce from this country will be safe, will be pure, will
be suitable for customers, and will meet every one of their expectations, including
safety.
Clearly, we have had a probl em here. A mistake has been made and we could spend
a lot of time here trying to analyse time lines and what went on and what could have
been done. The most important thing now is  that we support the Government, the
Government agencies, and Fonterra to ge t out around the world to explain how we
produce our milk and milk products in this country, and to give people an assurance that
the systems are fine.
There are, of course, questions starting to emerge today from China news sites—
questions around the laissez-faire market id eology that does determine some of the
current thinking by Government. In our own pa pers we have got: “Is Fonterra Too Big
For Its Gumboots?”. Then we have another reference here to Fonterra harming New
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12341
Zealand and itself. We know these things. That is why it is important that we act
together to resolve this as quickly as possible.
Fonterra is our single biggest company. We are proud of it. It is  the single biggest
exporter of anything from this country a nd our economy relies upon it. It is a hybrid
cooperative. In this House rece ntly we made changes to le gislation that did expand a
number of the masters that Fonterra should answer to. As a pure cooperative, it was first
and foremost to answer to its farmers, and that was the traditional way of thinking. The
new world, which both farmers and the new unit holders thr ough Trading Among
Farmers realise, is that it firstly must be responsible to its consumers, to its customers—
the people who buy its products—and must alwa ys keep in mind that the health and
safety of those consumers and of its workers should be its highest priority.
The farmers who have owned this compa ny, and who do so along with unit holders,
investors, today, are aware of the emerging, as  I say, reality of soci al media, of media
and communication that can send around the wo rld at a flash any concern that might
emerge from Fonterra’s operations and from its products, and they have to be on top of
that reality. Nothing should be hidden from th e processes and the products that Fonterra
produces in this country. As I say, I think the priority that Fonterra must state clearly to
the public—more often perhaps to politicians—is th at the health and safety of its
consumers through its products, and the health and safety of its workers at its worksites,
is the No. 1 priority for it. Production, growt h, and profit are all th ings that flow from
good management, and I wish Fonterra all the very best with that.
I think it is important to poi nt out the growth that the da iry industry has sustained. It
has helped this country grow, but it does cr eate some reality, I guess, for those looking
at Fonterra from the outside . In 1990 the whole dairy indu stry produced about half a
million tonnes of product for the world ma rkets. About 5 per cent of their total
production gets consumed in New Zealand and that has been consistent right
throughout. This year the company will export to the world about 2.7 million tonnes of
product. There has been, from some farming leaders, reference to  the fact that the
tonnage involved here—38 tonne s—is a very, very small pe rcentage of that total
production. That is true. None the less, that  small amount of contaminated production is
something that the world is focusing on and we are focusing on, and we have to get that
sorted out.
One of the questions I have raised—it is no t cheap politics but it is a real question—
is about the Government agency, the Ministry for Primary Industries, and its ability and
capability to get alongside Fonterra to help re solve this as quickly as possible. I did go
and look at the funding for that agency to ask whether it has been funded, because I was
encouraged by the Prime Minister’s statem ent that all possible resources will be
committed to resolving this and to reassuring our customers. The question I must ask,
and it is one that will be answered down the track, is whether the actual cutback in
funding for the Ministry for Pr imary Industries has been at the right time, when the
dairy industry growth has been so phenomenal.
We have had a meat industry report—ag ain, meat striking trouble and some
challenges getting into the Chinese market—t hat identified that there were insufficient
resources to properly follow th rough with the changes in accreditation and assurances
that the Chinese market needed. The questi on I ask, and it is for the Government to
answer at some stage in the future, is whether the cutback in funding from, indeed, $427
million in 2008 to $417 million in 2013 at a time  of rapid growth, particularly into
markets, has, perhaps, in some way contributed to this.
I go back. As I say, we are s upporting the Prime Minister. He has given an assurance
that all possible resources will be used. Our leader, David Shearer, has said that there
needs to be questions asked of Fonterra’s systems and the interaction. There will be
12342 Urgent Debates 6 Aug 2013
time for that. Of course, the Minister for Food Safety, Nikki Kaye, said that Ministry for
Primary Industries staff would be placed at Fonterra sites. That is welcomed. One of the
issues may be—because the reality is that th e dairy industry is a se lf-regulated industry,
unlike many others in the food industry—whe ther the Government is considering
moving back to slightly more regulation.
There will be international observers. Th ey will not be watching us here in the
House—they do not have to endure that—but they will be looking for assurances from
Parliament, and I think it is important to gi ve assurances. We ta ke food safety very
seriously. This is a piece of le gislation that is due to be back before Parliament to be
passed, and which governs the way that we d eal with all food in this country. Rest
assured we have good legislation.
The focus, as I say, on safety for c onsumers and workers must be the primary
consideration. Indeed, it is the primary c onsideration after a few lessons around worker
safety that we have learnt, but particularly  around food safety. It is the No. 1 focus and
priority, and it is committed to and supported by all parties in this House.
The second thing is that we have good sy stems of food production in this country.
They may not be perfect, but anyone in the international market place can be assured
that they are next to perfect, and that, in fact, what we have identified here through an
audit process, through testing,  is that we have had a prob lem. That is something that
acknowledges that the systems do work. We have got a healthy democracy. We have
got a robust system of accountability back to  Parliament. All the food produced in this
country will ultimately be observed, tested, audited, and checked by Parliament, and our
customers should be sure that we will be looking after their interests in the long term.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I want to, firstly, commend our team of
Ministers for what obviously has been a very strong response to a very difficult
situation. For New Zealand this is a critical is sue. It alerts us to the importance of the
dairy industry to New Zealand and, more important, it has reminded us of the
importance of food safety to this country.
Today I had the opportunity to ask Minister Groser what reports he had received of
international reaction to the potential cont amination of whey protein concentrate and
what measures the Government will be taking to reassure overseas markets and
consumers of our position. The Minister of  Trade’s answers and knowledge of these
issues reinforce the expertise that this count ry has and has been ab le to apply to this
most critical of issues. I think, again, I wa nt to commend the whole team of Ministers
who have put a lot of work into this issue over the last 3 days. It is particularly
important to this country.
I think also worth noting are the efforts of  the chief executive of Fonterra, who was
on the plane to China as quickly as he c ould be, and although there is a significant
amount of work to be done to understand the ramifications of this issue and what caused
this issue, I think Fonterra has reacted in a manner that is befitt ing its place in this
whole issue.
It is worth noting again the Prime Minister ’s statement that now is not the time for
recrimination. Now is the time to ensure that consumers have the best information
possible available to them. Ho wever, having said that, we  need to understand in the
fullness of time the reasons for the initial uncertainty, the reasons this contamination
took place, and the reasons that, I guess, th ere was some uncertainty about the timing of
the announcements that were made as a consequence of that.
It also reinforces for New Zealand the n eed to track all of our product and part
products from paddock to plate. That is so mething that our food industries, our meat
industry and all other aspects of our food i ndustry, have been particularly fussy about,
and something, of course, that the Natio nal Animal Identification and Tracing
6 Aug 2013 Urgent Debates 12343
legislation enforced, or reinforced, for the cattle industry in New Zealand, and it is no
doubt an issue that will follow into many other of our products or paddock-placed
products that end up on the plate in this countr y. So it is really important that we have
that traceability and that we understand where those products have gone.
I referred in the course of that little discussion to the part products. Of course, the
dairy industry is a manufacturer  of numerous part products  that make up end products.
This is the issue that we face with this whey product here today. It is a product of which
very small parts can be added to all sorts of things, from energy drinks to milk replacer
products and, in fact, to calf milk products . That is another pr oduct that has been
recalled in the course of this process.
Because of the nature of this country we ar e all feeling the effects of this. We are all
feeling for those parents of possibly aff ected children. We are all affected by any
possible damage to our reputation as a produc er of great food products. We rely on our
reputation for our future and our country’s liv ing. I have listened carefully to all the
debate, comment, and questions on this issu e today, and I would like to commend all
speakers for their constructive input. I also wa nt to add, having listened to all speakers
today, that were I a mother, father, or memb er of the public, I w ould feel I had been
much better briefed on this topic as a result of today’s discussion. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: E ng ā mana, e ng ā reo, e ng ā
kārangaranga maha o ng ā hau e wh ā. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. It is
with honour and humility that  I stand in Aotearoa New Zealand’s House of
Representatives as the member for Ikaroa-R āwhiti. I wish to first thank and
acknowledge the many wh ānau, iwi, and friends who are here in the public gallery and
who have travelled to join me in  this historic moment today. T ēnā koutou. To my
parliamentary predecessors who passed the M āori Representation Act 1867, which led
to the formation of the four M āori seats—Northern, Western, Southern, and our own
beloved Eastern—and to the inaugural member who held the Eastern seat, T āreha Te
Moananui, and to the first M āori woman member, Iriaka Matiu R ātana, kei te mihi, kei
te mihi. To my fellow Māori MPs in the House today, tēnā koutou katoa.
Our nation is founded on the blood, sweat, and toil of generations of men and women
who worked the land, on our wharves, in th e freezing works, the shearing sheds, with
railways, and in forestry to  build our nation and our econom y into the stronghold that it
is today. In 1916 the New Zealand Labour Party was founded on a single kaupapa: to be
the voice of change for the working-class pe ople. As this nation has evolved so has the
party. But the founding prin ciples remain the same: to  care for the poor and the
disenfranchised, and to speak up for thos e within our community who cannot for
themselves. In 1935 in the first Labour-led Government the Rt Hon Michael Savage, in
his wisdom, formed a polit ical alliance with the R ātana Church, a precursory step to
forming an allegiance with iwi Māori.
The bond between the New Zealand Labour Pa rty and the electo rate of Ikaroa-
Rāwhiti is unique and entrenched in its ow n right. From 1943 to 1996 and from 1999
until today, Ikaroa-R āwhiti has entrusted the Labour Part y to advocate for the rights of
its people; a relationship that expands some 70 years. But I state this as a friendly
reminder: this historic relationship should never be taken for granted. The relationship
between iwi M āori and Labour-led Governments has progressed considerably since
1935. Under Labour the M āori Trade Training scheme was introduced, Te Reo M āori
was recognised as an official language, and under the strong influence of the Hon Matiu
12344 Maiden Statements 6 Aug 2013
Rata the Waitangi Tribunal was established to address Treaty grievances. However, iwi
Māori have not forgotten the chal lenges to this relationship in recent times, particularly
with the introduction of the foreshor e and seabed legislation and the T ūhoe raids.
Despite these challenges it is now time to m ove forward, and to shift our focus to what
lies ahead of us as a part y and as a nation, towards th e game-changer known as the
Māori economy.
The Ikaroa-Rāwhiti electorate extends from the East Cape of the North Island to the
Wellington region, and includes Gi sborne, Hawke’s Bay, and the Wairarapa, as well as
most of the Hutt Valley and Wainui ōmata. Almost one-quarter of these residents in
Ikaroa-Rāwhiti speak Te Reo M āori. This compares with barely 4 percent in New
Zealand overall. Over one-quarter of thos e employed in the electorate are in the
agriculture, forestry, fishing, and manufacturing sectors. We have strong iwi within the
electorate: Ngati Porou, Te Aitanga-a-M āhaki, Rongowhakaata, Ngai T āmanuhiri,
Rongomaiwahine, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Rangitāne and Te Ātiawa.
During the 6 weeks leading into the by-elec tion I had the opportunity to speak to our
people, who were clear with me about the needs of wh ānau. Our people need jobs. Our
rangatahi need opportunities he re at home. Our kuia and kaum ātua need access to
quality health services. Everyone deserves a warm, affordable home. Everyone deserves
a fair go. The national unemployment rate is 6.8 percent, but for M āori in the Hawke’s
Bay unemployment is two times that, at 13.8 percent. Long-term unemployment on the
East Coast has increased from 10.9 percent in December 2008 to 19.8 percent in March
2013. In the Wellington region, which includes the Hutt Valley, unemployment went
from 3.6 percent in December 2008 to 7.9 percent in December 2012—that is an
increase of 9,600 people who are une mployed. The people of Ikaroa-R āwhiti need
quality, sustainable jobs. The manuf acturing sector, which employs many M āori, has
taken a hammering in my electorate: 125 j obs at Cedenco Foods in Gisborne in 2009
gone; 304 jobs at Ovation meatworks in Wai pukurau in 2011 gone; this year 70 jobs at
New Zealand Post Petone gone; and between 50 to 80 jobs at Godfrey Hirst’s woollen
mill in Dannevirke gone. The flow-on effects of these job losses on wh ānau and small
communities are devastating. The people of Ikaroa-R āwhiti need quality, sustainable
jobs.
So what can be done? Local solutions to  local problems wo rking with local
champions is a community development appro ach focusing on job creations that I have
seen work successfully in times of despai r. There are many local champions on limited
resources doing their bit to he lp those most in need. I sa lute our community advocates,
unions, churches, schools, businesses, marae, and iwi Māori organisations, including the
Māori Women’s Welfare League and the M āori Wardens Association, for your
compassion, caring, and sense of community  commitment. Regional development is
critical to the success of th e nation’s sustainable economic growth, and more needs to
be done at the regional level. In Ikaroa-R āwhiti it is about people as  much as it is about
market drivers. Oil exploration and dams that wipe out complete valleys are not
sustainable. There are alternatives, and gr eater investment in regional research and
development will show that. Developing hi gh-level strategic goals with community
movers and shakers encourages ownership and, therefore, commitment.
I worked for many years in the Community Employment Group of the former
Department of Labour. We were as diverse as the communities we supported. Company
Rebuilders—retired executives who work w ith many company owners on the brink of
closure to keep them afloat and, by associ ation, save jobs. Supe r Grans—retired people
who assisted young people with budget advice  and meal preparation. Our “Labour
shock response team” provided much-need ed coordination and support when sudden
job loss announcements were made, through es tablishing temporary resource centres to
6 Aug 2013 Maiden Statements 12345
help with finding alternative employment, career counselling, and CV preparation. And
Mainstreet, a small-town renewable initiative, showed that with a lick of paint and a few
pot plants, out-of-towners would stop in small towns where once they would drive
through, bringing much-needed money to the local economy.
A similar approach was taken with a small community whose major employer closed
its doors, leaving nothing to absorb the many redundant locals. Every community has a
unique point of difference, and after a series of community planning meetings the locals
in casual conversations joked about how whales visiting their coastline was their unique
point of difference. The rest  is history. Whale Watch Kaik ōura is now a multimillion-
dollar business that not only employs many lo cals but has almost single-handedly been
the catalyst for economic growth in Kaik ōura and the surrounding district. So what can
we learn from these initiatives, from this a pproach? Government has an enabling role to
support hapū, iwi, and communities to create sustainable solutions for wh ānau. The key
word here is “enable”.
This era is the beginning of a M āori economic renaissance, and recognises the Māori
economic powerbase that has been fought for by wh ānau, hapū, and iwi on the streets,
in the courts, and most recently at the ne gotiating tables with the Office of Treaty
Settlements. I pay homage to the many men and women, some no longer with us, who
have worked tirelessly in pursuit of justi ce and equity through the Treaty settlement
process. It would be remiss of  me not to acknowledge the Hon Michael Cullen, the late
Hon Parekura Horomia, and, more recently, fr om the opposite side of the House, the
Hon Christopher Finlayson for their collective commitment to settling Treaty
grievances.
The role of iwi M āori in a post-settlement era is to  grow and protect its asset base
and to create intergenerational wealth. Innovative iwi M āori are exploring opportunities
and how these opportunities provide wider returns. Ng āti Wh ātua has committed to
getting its own people into affordable and sustainable homes, and Ng āti Kahungunu has
recently purchased Tautāne farm to act as a catalyst to unlock the economic potential of
other land blocks, to provide an investment opportunity for recently settled hapū groups,
and, ultimately, to provide jobs.
Investing and creating opportunities fo r their own people is unquestionably
applaudable, but is it not the responsibility of iwi M āori alone. The role of Government
is to enable innovation that will create jobs . Tailored regional investment in areas like
research and development, technical internships, and encouraging multipartite
arrangements including iwi M āori, local government, busin esses, schools, and unions
will accelerate this form of innova tion, just like the Whale Watch Kaik ōura example. I
am convinced that what is good for iwi M āori economic development is good for the
nation as a whole. If this gr eat nation of ours is looking for a game-changer, then I am
offering one: regional investment  in partnership with iwi M āori to unlock inherent
opportunities that will create r eal jobs throughout the elect orate and for the people of
Ikaroa-Rāwhiti. I come into this House with a co mmitment to work with any party that
has policies that work—policies that create sustainable jobs, warm and affordable
homes, quality health services , and clear pathways, be it in  education, training, or jobs
for our rangatahi and people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
I was raised in a loving wh ānau, surrounded by values-based role models, many who
shaped who I am today. I wish to acknowledge  some of them. Firstly, I would like to
acknowledge my great-grandmother Reremo ana Hakiwai née Paratene, who gave
relentless service and unconditi onal love to her family, to her faith, and to her beloved
Hukarere Girls’ College. On behalf of my  late great-grandmother and the Hukarere
community, we need to complete the chap el. Her daughter, my grandmother Ruruhira
Robin née Nepe Apat ū, known affectionately as Aunt y Lulu, was renowned for her
12346 Maiden Statements 6 Aug 2013
ability to keep our men, when speaking from  the paepae, from straying off topic with a
certain glare. Suffer fools she did not. And my dear uncle Pong Wy llie, father of the
former member for Te Tai Tonga, T ūtekawa, who taught me th e value of work—hard
work. A man who never minced his words, his brutal honesty and cheeky charm would
disarm the most disconcerting amongst us. He  taught me that there are no shortcuts in
life—you get out what you put in. Fi nally, the late Hon Parekura T ūreia Horomia, who
taught me to love our people, to serve our people, and, amongst all else, “hold the line”.
In summary, I have spoken about the real issues facing our people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
I have spoken today about the hist oric relationship between Ikaroa-R āwhiti, the New
Zealand Labour Party, and the Government . I have highlighted the challenges and,
moreover, identified emerging opportunities and an  approach that would assist to create
sustainable quality jobs in a post-settlement era.
To every single person who supported me throughout the arduous and well-fought
by-election, thank you for your dedication, comm itment, and heart to retain the Ikaroa-
Rāwhiti electorate. To my fellow Labour caucu s colleagues—in particular our leader,
David Shearer, Moana Mackey, Nanaia Mahuta, and Annette King—thank you for your
time, your resource, your energy, and your wisdom you gave my wh ānau and me on the
election trail. To my parents, W īremu and May Whaitiri, thank you for your love, thank
you for your sacrifices, and thank you for th e opportunities you provide d to all five of
your children, and for carrying on that comm itment to our children, your mokopuna. To
my sister Joanne Rowe, who besides bein g the typical big sister was for 14 years
Parekura’s out-of-office support. You and your girls went to extraordinary lengths to
support him over the years—none more than  over his last few months. From the
electorate, thank you very much for caring fo r our chief Parekura. To my sons Nohorua
and WīRangi, thank you for being awesome young men. The world is both your oyster,
and all I ask is that you make the most of your opportuni ties at school, on the sports
fields, and particularly in your next YouTube clip for ne xt year’s general election.
Finally, to my partner Kiritapu Lyndsay A llan, your unconditional love and support
know no end. Thank you for all that you are; thank you for all that you will be.
I am proud to stand before this House as th e Labour Party member of Parliament and
the first elected woman for the Eastern and Ikaroa-R āwhiti electorate. As a mother, a
daughter, and product of hard manual-labourin g parents I present myself to the New
Zealand House of Representatives as a humble servant of the people of Ikaroa-R āwhiti
and to our great nation Aotearoa New Zealand. May I be judged on my actions and held
accountable to those whom I seek to represent. N ō reira, e te iwi, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.
Waiata
Sitting suspended from 5.54 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

sections.heading: Government Communications Security Bureau And Related

items.text: Referral to Government Administration Committee

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I move, That the Government
Communications Security Bureau and Rela ted Legislation Amendment Bill be
discharged to the Government Administ ration Committee for its consideration,
including hearing the Police, SIS, Defe nce Force, Government Communications
Security Bureau, and any other appropriate agencies.
6 Aug 2013 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bill 12347
A party vote was called for on the question, That the motion be agreed to.
Ayes 57
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Party 14 ; New Zealand First 7; Mana 1;

items.speaker: Independent
items.text: Horan.
Noes 64
New Zealand National 59; M āori Party 3; ACT New Zealand 1; Independent:
Dunne.
Motion not agreed to.
In Committee
Part 1  Amendments to Government Communications Security Bureau Act 2003

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Part 1 of the
Government Communications Security Bur eau and Related Legislation Amendment
Bill deals with amendments to the Government Communica tions Security Bureau Act
2003. I thought it would be helpful if I outli ned to the Committee 12 key aspects of the
changes that are set out in the bill. The purpos e of these changes is to provide a clearly
formulated and consistent statutory framework, to create a greater oversight regime, and
to update the Act to respond to the changing security environment.
As I say, there are 12 key aspects. The first deals with definitions and interpretation.
If one looks at section 4 of the 2003 Act, one sees that it contains definitions of various
terms that are now outdated and require replacement, amendment, or repeal. They
include definitions of “computer syst em”, “foreign communications”, “foreign
intelligence”, and “network”. The amendm ent bill inserts a new definition for
“information infrastructure” to replace th e definitions of “computer system” and
“network” and to take into account the new ways in which communications are carried
and stored. The definition is a broad one, and it  is there to make sure all the ways of
communication are indeed captured.
The next key aspect I wish to tell the Committee about de als with clause 6. Sections
7 and 8 of the 2003 Act are replaced. The fi rst is the objective of the Government
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB). Th e current objective section is a lengthy
statement of what the bureau contributes to  in the interests of New Zealand. The bill
proposes an objective clause based on the cu rrent section but gr eatly simplified and
clearer. So the bureau will contribute to the national security, international well-being,
and so on. Then we have a replacement for s ection 8, dealing with the functions of the
bureau. Section 8 of the 2003 Act sets out three functions: foreign intelligence,
information assurance and cyber-security, and cooperation and assistance to other
entities. What has happened here is that this aspect of the functions of the bureau is spelt
out a lot more clearly.
The bill repeals and replaces section 8 with four new sections, sections 8A to 8D.
They set out the three functions more clearl y and specify the limitations and restrictions
that apply to each of those functions, so fo reign intelligence is covered by section 8B,
information assurance and cyber-security by section 8A, and cooperation and assistance
to other entities by section 8C. It is very  important to focus on section 8C and the
greater restrictions and lim itations that are put around this  function. The agencies that
can be assisted are limited to three named agencies and the bureau is going to be subject
to the limitations, restrictions, and oversight that the requesting agency is subjected to.
The Hon Mr Dunne has a Supplementary Order Paper, Supplementary Order Paper 308,
that is going to tighten up that aspect even more.
12348 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bill 6 Aug 2013
I then come to the principl es of the legislation. In act ual fact, the 2003 Act does not
contain any principles, but the bureau, as a core public sector department, comes under
the provisions of the State Sector Ac t 1988, which means it is subject to the Public
Service Code of Conduct . Section 8CA sets out the principles underpinning the
performance of the bureau’s functions. An e xplicit set of principles is inserted, and
these are modelled on the principles inserted in the New Zealand Security Intelligence
Service Act 1969.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Who’s going to enforce them? How are they going to be enforced?
Who will know?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Those principles include acting in
accordance with the law and human rights sta ndards and in a manner that facilitates
effective oversight. A nother important point, I say to Mr Little, is that there is a
requirement in section 8CA that the director  must regularly consult the Leader of the
Opposition.
Then we have provisions re lating to the appointment of a director. The current Act
provides that the director is appointed by the Governor-General on the recommendation
of the Prime Minister. Cabinet decided in 2010 to involve the State Services
Commissioner in managing the appointment  process. This was done through the
Cabinet Manual, pending an opportunity for the review of the legislation, and so the bill
incorporates the Cabinet Manual  process into statute, making the management of the
appointment more transparent. The same pr ocess provisions are going to be inserted
into the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Act.
The next clause, clause 12, is  a critical clause dealing with section 14. The bureau is
not to target New Zealanders’ private communications. The current section 14 was
intended to codify the basic premise underp inning the bureau’s operations. However,
the way the basic premise was incorporated in to the Act meant that it applied not only
to the foreign intelligence function but also  to its two other functions—unfortunately,
some sloppy drafting there. So the bill retain s the fundamental premise but section 14 is
amended to make it clear that it does not a pply to cyber-security or to cooperation and
assistance. Where New Zealanders’ commun ications are to be intercepted, then
additional safeguards have been put in place.
The next aspect concerns warrantless pow ers. The current Act provides for the
interception of communicati ons without a warrant in ce rtain limited circumstances.
Those warrantless powers are retained, but are further restricted. The bill makes it clear
that the warrantless powers cannot be used if a New Zealander is involved. The next
provision I want to talk about concerns  warrants and authoris ations. I refer the
Committee to the existing sections 17 and 18. The bill repeals those provisions and
replaces them with clearer and more consistent provisions set out in a better order, and I
refer honourable members to sections 15A to 15F, in clause 14. Significant new
limitations are added, in particular a re quirement that any warrants involving New
Zealanders must be issued jointly by the Minister and the Commi ssioner of Security
Warrants, and, more important, that priv ileged communications—legal, medical, and
religious—as set out in the Evidence Act 2006, cannot be targeted.
Under the existing legislation there is no requirement for record keeping, but under
the proposed legislation the information must be recorded for every warrant and be put
in a statutory register available at any time for the Inspector-General of Intelligence and
Security and the Minister to review. Mr Dunne’s Supplementary Order Paper will
provide some further information in that regard.
Very important, under the existing legislation on the subject of immunities, there is
an immunity provision, but its effect is uncertain and unclear. The new legislation
tightens this up, and there is an immunity provision that, basically, is modelled on the
6 Aug 2013 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bill 12349
Search and Surveillance Act 2012. That immu nity provision is not absolute. A bureau
employee will still be subject to legal proceedings if he or she acts in bad faith,
unreasonably, or outside their powers.
I have two final points. One concerns inci dentally obtained intelligence. The current
Act allows intelligence about New Zealanders that is incidentally obtained during
foreign intelligence operations to be communi cated to other people if it relates to
serious crime. Section 25 of the Act is replaced to make it clearer when, and with
whom, such intelligence can be shared. Th e intelligence can be communicated only to
public authorities.
And, finally, there is the issue of protec tion of personal information. The bureau is
currently exempt from prin ciples 1, 5, 8, and 9 of the Privacy Act 1993. In 2011 the
Law Commission recommended that those principles should apply, and so the bill
addresses that issue. The director will be required, in consultation with the Privacy
Commissioner and the Inspector-General of In telligence and Security, to formulate a
policy on the protection and disclosure of personal information that complies with those
principles. So they are the 12 key aspects, a nd I think it would be very helpful if we
could address those.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The last point in that 12-long list
from the previous speaker, Chris Finlayson, is , I think, particularly relevant in light of
what happened today in the protection of private communications and private property.
We had the Prime Minister just 2 weeks ago telling us that he had nothing to do with the
handing over of a journalist’s private communi cations, and here we have him today,
knowing that the chief executive officer of hi s own department, whom he seems not to
talk to at all, has actually been in the possession of emails of a journalist and Peter
Dunne for a very long time. Going through that  episode just emphasises what this bill,
the Government Communications Security Bureau and Related Legislation Amendment
Bill, is all about. It is about the balance be tween security and priv acy, and if there was
one incident of that in the past few weeks, it was that on 31 July—last week—the Prime
Minister said something, and something else  was the case when they dumped all those
emails on Friday. That really is the reason why we are not supporting this bill.
This bill has been rushed through. It has not been informed well enough. It has not
stood the test of what we would expect in order to change the legislation in the way that
it actually has been. We, for example, asked for the SIS, the New Zealand Police, and
the Ministry of Defence to appear before the Intelligence and Security Committee. None
of those agencies was permitted to appear before the committee, because the chair, who
has the casting vote, said he did not want them to. Why? Because he wanted to rush this
legislation through without us being able to get much better information. And that is the
reason that the balance between privacy a nd security is completely the wrong way
round.
The Prime Minister says that, as part of this  bill, we have all the checks and balances
there. But let me tell you this: the Prime Minister, as we found out earlier this year,
appoints the head of the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) and the
SIS. That person happens to be his friend and meets with him one on one without
anybody else around. One on one they meet toge ther. The Prime Minister also sits on
the oversight committee, the Intelligence and Security Committee. He chairs that
committee, he has the casting vote, he sets the agenda, and if anybody wants to put any
other item on that agenda—as Russel Norman and I well know—of course it is voted
down. It is immediately voted down. The Prim e Minister also appoints the Inspector-
General of Intelligence and S ecurity, who looks in to these affairs, and he appoints the
Commissioner of Security Warrants, who issues the warrants to spy on New Zealanders.
12350 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bill 6 Aug 2013
I do not want to impugn the integrity of those people who have been appointed to
those positions, but what we have is a system  that is not about checks and balances; it is
about one man holding that authority. And if there is any demonstration of how that
authority can be abused, it has been in the last few weeks when that Prime Minister
blamed a contractor for handing over ema ils and phone records. Today what we are
finding is that it was not about  a contractor; it was actually  about the Prime Minister’s
own office asking for those emails and thos e phone records. Not only that but those
emails and phone records came in and were held by the Department of the Prime
Minister and Cabinet for over 3 or 4 weeks without the Prime Minister being told. Well,
we are told that by the Prime Minister. Ther e are only three options, really: firstly, that
the Prime Minister is not te lling the truth about being in formed by the Department of
the Prime Minister and Cabinet; secondly, that he is woefully ignorant of what is going
on in terms of what is actually happening, and that person is not handing over the
information he needs, which means that it is an incompetent department that he is
running; or, thirdly, that he has actually e xplicitly told people: “Don’t tell me. I don’t
want to know.” because it is a whole lot bett er not to know. He did this with the John

items.speaker: Banks report by saying
items.text: “I don’t want to read that police report, b ecause then I’ll have
to know, and then I’ll have to do something about John Banks.” [Bell rung] Mr Chair—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am just going to make a comment, if the
member would like to resume his seat. I unde rstand that this is a matter about which
there is some contention, but the standard in  Committee is that we are debating Part 1. I
will give the member another call, but we ought  to be debating Part 1. This is not a
general debate.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I am getting to Part 1. It took a little
longer to get through the context to get to Part 1. Part 1 is about the appointment of the
head of the GCSB. What we are saying is that we are submitting Supplementary Order
Paper 305, a Supplementary Order Paper that  calls for an inde pendent, wide-ranging
inquiry within 1 month of this law passing—if,  indeed, it unfortunately does pass. What
that would mean is that an inquiry would be set up. The terms of reference would be
agreed right across Parliament. The inquiry would have at least three persons on it—
persons of standing, people who are able to command respect in their fields. Our
Supplementary Order Paper would also introduce a sunset clause into this bill so that
the bill would expire within 12 months, so that an inquiry would be able to go through.
It would be able to have the appropriate amount of consultation, we would be able to
draft and push through a new law based on th at inquiry, and the current legislation
would simply sink into the sunset, as “sunset clause” suggests. That enables us to have
the law round the right way, rather than the wrong way.
What we are trying to do now is to charge  ahead and fix a bill that is being rushed
through in response to a political problem, not  a bill that comes from the good evidence
and good recommendations that would come from an inquiry. That has been our
position from day one. It has been our position from the end of last year. Unfortunately,
we are not likely to get this law stopped, because Peter Dunne, who is here in the
Chamber listening to this, has given Mr Key—what is the expression—he has sold his
vote, and Mr Key was a willing buyer of hi s vote. As Mr Key said to me: “We need
only one vote to get across the line.” This is what he means by consensus: “Yes, you
can come in with us if you lik e, but, actually, I’ve  got the votes, so you don’t need to.”
That is consensus. Is it picking up the phone ? No. Is it office to office communication?
No. Was there any form of communication be tween us initiated by Mr Key because he
wants this bill to have more cross-party s upport? No, absolutely not. He has got that
vote, all he wants is that vote, and it is ju st about getting Mr Dunne, the willing seller of
his vote, across the floor.
6 Aug 2013 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bill 12351
It is deeply ironic that Mr Dunne right now is deeply immersed in the current goings-
on and the shenanigans of this Prime Mini ster, who is misleading Parliament and
misleading the public—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Come back to the bill.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: —about his role in this bill. Mr  Dunne is still supporting this
legislation. He is supporting Pa rt 1, including the appointment of the head of the GCSB
by the Prime Minister, despite what has happe ned and despite the fact that his personal
emails have been accessed. Who knows whethe r they have been l ooked at, because the
GCSB, the subject of the bill we are deba ting here today, certain ly has the powers to
open attachments. I have no doubt about that . The Department of the Prime Minister
and Cabinet might not be able to open an attachment, but I can be very sure that the
GCSB has those sets of skills that enable us to do that.
Supplementary Order Paper 305 does what we  believe is the righ t thing to do. It
starts by providing for a proper inquiry into  our intelligence agencies—not just the
GCSB but right across the board. It brings to the fore something that we have not had an
independent inquiry on since 1976. That wa s the last time we had any independent
inquiry into our intelligence agencies. Many, many people are sa ying to me that this is
exactly what we need to do. From there we move to the legislative change that is
necessary to set up a structure that woul d have the confidence of New Zealanders,
because right now this bill certainly—

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I just want to pick up where
David Shearer left off, about the fact that what the Government would purport that this
Government Communications Security Bur eau and Related Legislation Amendment
Bill does is, in fact, restore the confidence in the Government Communications Security
Bureau (GCSB) that has been lost. The real ity is that, under the watch of John Key,
public confidence in the GCSB has dropped to an  all-time low. The reality is that this
bill, and in particular Part 1 of this bill, will do nothing to restore the confidence of New
Zealanders in the GCSB. In large part, that is because the Prime Minister has said, and
claimed right throughout this debate, that this bill does not extend the powers of the
GCSB. That is a completely laughable clai m. Almost every submitter who came before
the Intelligence and Security Committee, the statutory committee—every submitter bar
one who came in front of that committee—said: “This extends the powers of the GCSB,
and there is no case being made for it.” Not only is the Prime Mini ster just plain wrong
and misleading New Zealanders by  trying to say that this is  just a clarification of the
legislation, that is what the explanatory not e of this bill says; it says this is a
clarification. It is not. It is an extension of the powers of the GCSB without justification
from this Government.
When we look at the case that the Government has made for this, we see that it knew
about problems with spying—a rguably illegal s pying—last year. Was there an urgent
piece of legislation put into the Parliament saying that New Zealanders’ lives were in
danger and we needed to ensure that the powers of the GCSB were extended? No. The
Government tried to cover that up in itially, through the Prime Minister. When,
eventually, it was forced out into the open, we went through the process that we went
through to get this bill up now, and then th e Prime Minister had a sudden rush of
urgency. That is when John Key suddenly deci ded that the whole thing was incredibly
urgent, because it was time for him to stick a band-aid ove r the wound to this
Government that is the GCSB.
